💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term.
  • The border has been secured, deportations have been carried out at a high rate, federal agencies have been forced to abandon much of their institutional commitment to DEI and financial support of the left-wing NGO complex, universities have been put on notice that federal funding is not unconditional, and the administrative state has undergone its most serious shake-up in generations.
  • Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

It has been revealed that the catastrophic midterm results dealt to Republicans two weeks ago threaten but do not ultimately negate the conservative policy landscape as it stands two years into President Trump’s second term. As I wrote before the election, many aspects of this administration are clearly good from the conservative perspective, not just by comparison to the Biden administration, but to Trump’s own first term and previous Republican administrations since the days of Ronald Reagan.

The border has been secured, deportations have been carried out at a high rate, federal agencies have been forced to abandon much of their institutional commitment to DEI and financial support of the left-wing NGO complex, universities have been put on notice that federal funding is not unconditional, and the administrative state has undergone its most serious shake-up in generations.

Inez Feltscher Stepman is a senior policy and legal analyst at the Independent Women's Forum.

On “Can Trump’s Agenda Survive the Blue Tsunami?”.

Latest Update: United partner TAP adding a 2nd Portugal route from Washington, DC

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Washingtonians have a newly introduced option to Portugal next summer.
  • TAP Air Portugal will launch a upcoming thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027.
  • Industry observers note that TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the latest IAD-OPO route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Washingtonians have a newly introduced option to Portugal next summer.

TAP Air Portugal will launch a upcoming thrice-weekly service from Dulles International Airport (IAD) to Porto Airport (OPO) on March 30, 2027. Westbound flights will operate on Wednesdays, Fridays and Saturdays through the summer, and on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays beginning in October.

Industry observers note that TAP, a Star Alliance partner of United Airlines, will fly an Airbus A321LR on the latest IAD-OPO route. The long-range, single-aisle aircraft is fitted with 16 lie-flat business-class seats and 155 economy seats.

Sources indicate that the new Portugal route is the latest international addition at IAD. United prepares to launch new service to Toulouse, France, in April and to Milan in May, using its new long-range A321XLR on the former route.

International seats from IAD will increase nearly 7% in the first six months of 2027 compared to this year, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium highlights.

In a recent development, IAD is undergoing a massive, $22 billion redevelopment to bring its infrastructure up to modern standards. The first piece — a 14-gate section of the new Concourse E that includes a new, large United Club — opened earlier in November. Future phases include a new international arrivals facility that would support additional long-haul growth.

This content is hosted by Instagram.

And if the redevelopment plan stays on schedule, IAD could retire its jet-age mobile lounges by the mid-2030s.

TAP’s new OPO route complements its existing service to IAD from Lisbon Airport (LIS).

It has been revealed that the state-owned Portuguese airline is in the process of being privatized as part of the Lufthansa Group. The German airline conglomerate aims to buy an initial 44.9% stake in TAP, aiming to close the deal by the first quarter of 2028.

Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx mentioned in October that once the TAP deal is done, Lufthansa intends to integrate the Portuguese airline into its transatlantic joint venture with Air Canada and United.

Industry News: Amex Auto-Enrolling Card Members In Paperless Billing (Sorry, Dad!)

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
  • According to recent reports, with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
  • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

According to recent reports, with banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

Sources indicate that after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

Now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it says this:.

Recent findings suggest that not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

It has been revealed that it’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

Then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary says something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

It has been revealed that as of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

What do you make of Amex’s switch to paperless billing?

Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

You do not need a password and dual factor authentication every time you want to review a paper statement. Takes a lot longer to get to the statement online than just opening an envelope.

I still get paper statements and I'm sure the Post Office needs the business.

Ben I think you're very wrong with your comments that 99% of OMAAT users do not use paper statements. Like many commenters here, I greatly prefer paper statements and will jump through whatever hoops Amex sets up in order to keep receiving them. I am not 90 years old - I am a millennial. And I find it significantly easier to gather all of the paper statements I have received across 20+ credit cards, utilities, mortgage, and other accounts and pay them once every 2 weeks. It also makes it significantly easier to review the statements for fraudulent charges, refunds or other credits that may have posted incorrectly, etc. Statements are too easy to miss in email with all of the other messages that come in. I'm glad you alerted us to this so I can opt back in.

Sources indicate that chase does this too once in a while. Have to go into the account and undo paperless.

According to recent reports, saving posts is a member feature. Become an OMAAT member to build a reading list you can come back to from any device.

Why Virgin Atlantic Is Targeting The 40 RAF Pilots Keeping Britain's F-35 Fleet Flyable

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the United Kingdom only has around four dozen trained F-35B fighter jet pilots and around 150 Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet pilots.
  • As the Royal Air Force is so much smaller than the United States Air Force (and Marines/Navy), it lacks depth in pilots.
  • Sources indicate that with that being said, airlines will typically focus more on military transport pilots, such as those flying A330 MRTTs and A400Ms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the United Kingdom only has around four dozen trained F-35B fighter jet pilots and around 150 Eurofighter Typhoon fighter jet pilots. Losing even a handful of these hard-to-replace pilots to commercial airlines is painful. They are targeted by British airlines, with Virgin Atlantic directly targeting them in its recruitment ads in 2024.

As the Royal Air Force is so much smaller than the United States Air Force (and Marines/Navy), it lacks depth in pilots. Training an F-35 fighter jet pilot can cost around $10 million, and newly introduced pilots graduating annually in the UK are often measured in the single digits.

Sources indicate that with that being said, airlines will typically focus more on military transport pilots, such as those flying A330 MRTTs and A400Ms. Let's examine how Virgin Atlantic seeks to attract ex-RAF pilots and why this is a major problem for the Royal Air Force (and Royal Navy).

In 2024, the publication London Loves Business wrote that "RAF pilots who have operated on F-35 B Lightning II and Typhoon FGR4 are being offered double their annual salary to join Virgin." It adds that those pilots would be given routes to Barbados and Newly introduced York to quit the RAF and fly with Virgin Atlantic.

In a recent development, the report stated that the pilots were being offered around double the money that they would typically earn flying for the Royal Air Force. At the time, the Virgin Atlantic advert was reported to read as follows:.

Recent findings suggest that "In order to be suitable, you must be operating, or have operated in the last three years on one of the following RAF Aircraft: F-35 B Lightning II, Typhoon FGR4. As a member of our Flight Crew, you will be joining the UK’s only exclusively long-haul airline. Flying out of London Heathrow to exciting destinations such as Newly introduced York, San Francisco, Las Vegas, Delhi, Barbados, Antigua, and many more.".

In a recent development, the advert went on to say that Virgin Atlantic operates the "youngest, cleanest, and most technologically sophisticated" widebody aircraft. Virgin is unusual in exclusively operating a fleet of widebody aircraft. Airlines poaching trained fighter jet pilots is common in many countries, including the United States. For air forces, this can be devastating as it costs around ten million dollars to train a frontline fighter jet pilot and takes years to replace them.

In a typical Western air force, there should be around 1.3 to 1.5 trained pilots for every fast jet. That mentioned, Britain (and other air forces) have struggled to maintain this figure. While the US military has around 37,000 military pilots, including in the USAF, Army (helicopters), Marines, Navy, and Coast Guard, the British military likely has around 2,500.

In a recent development, of these, around 1,500 are in the RAF and 500 are each in the Royal Navy and British Army. In 2014, the British Government revealed that there were 1,760 trained regular pilots in the RAF (excluding reserves and other aircrew), although that number has likely declined somewhat over the last decade. However, fighter jet pilots are a small subset of the overall group of pilots.

In late 2022, former Defense Secretary Ben Wallace revealed there were only 30 qualified British F-35 pilots, plus three exchange pilots. By 2023, that number had risen to 34, with seven more soon to graduate. By mid-2026, the RAF had received all of its initially ordered 48 F-38Bs, minus one that fell off an aircraft carrier.

Ideally, the RAF should have around 60–70 or so trained F-35B pilots, but it is unclear how many there are. There have been reports that the ratio may be closer to one pilot per jet, suggesting the RAF may now have somewhere around 45 to 50 trained F-35B pilots. Headlines will often talk about the fighter jets, how many there are, and how ready they are, but pilot availability is often a more pressing bottleneck.

Industry observers note that the RAF procured a total of 137 Eurofighter Typhoons. Of these, 26 of the Tranche 1 fighter jets have now been retired, leaving a fleet of four remaining. These are stationed at RAF Mount Pleasant in the Falkland Islands as the UK's farthest air base with a permanent fighter jet presence. They are tasked with defending the islands from Argentina and are supported by A400Ms and A330 MRTTs.

In a recent development, the remaining Typhoons include 67 Tranche 2 and 40 Tranche 3 fighter jets. In January 2026, the British Government stated it would upgrade 40 of them with newly introduced radars and other systems. In July 2026, the budget was significantly increased, and it was reported that all would be upgraded. Britain had previously stated the remaining four Tranche 1 fighter jets would retire in 2027, but now it is unclear.

Select aircraft of the Royal Air Force (per RAF).

F-35Bs (shared with Royal Navy).

There has not been an equivalent public disclosure for how many Typhoon fighter jet pilots are serving in the RAF. A reasonable range would be 140-160 trained Typhoon pilots. This would give the RAF a group of up to 200 fast jet pilots in total. Additionally, as of June 2026, the Royal Air Force had 119 trainee fast-jet pilots progressing through the training pipeline, from RAF Cranwell to the point of starting an Operational Conversion Unit.

Beginning around 2015 and then accelerating after COVID-19, the US airline industry has faced an unprecedented pilot shortage. This has affected regional airlines in particular and is made worse by retiring baby boomers. In response, the industry moved to attract former US military helicopter pilots; previously, the focus had been on fixed-wing pilots.

One of the most famous examples was that of Frontier Airlines, which launched its Rotor Transition Program to help military helicopter pilots transition and receive their fixed-wing qualifications. The program ended up being so successful that, Frontier's website said:.

In a recent development, "Due to the overwhelmingly positive response and large number of applications we received for our Rotor Transition Program, we have temporarily closed the application window. Keep an eye out for more information regarding the application window opening and future recruitment events.".

Sources indicate that meanwhile, there has not been the same recruitment drive in the UK, as the UK airline industry is much smaller, the military is much smaller (only a few hundred helicopter pilots), and converting is less straightforward. Instead, British industry focuses on recruiting former RAF transport pilots, fast jet pilots, airline cadets, and airline pilots from other airlines.

Sources indicate that in both the United States and the United Kingdom, it is relatively straightforward for fighter jet pilots to transition from flying fixed-wing military aircraft to flying commercial passenger jets. With that being noted, the United States has built a considerably more mature and streamlined process.

For ex-British fast-jet pilots, the primary challenge is obtaining the civilian licenses, certifications, and experience required by the UK Civil Aviation Authority. The CAA does recognize military flying experience through its Military Aircrew Accreditation Scheme, meaning that transitioning pilots do not need to start from scratch.

They can get credits toward their Commercial Pilot License, but still generally need to complete their ATPL theoretical knowledge tests, civilian flight tests, and so on. The entire process of converting from military to commercial jets often takes six to twelve months, depending on how much training credit is granted and the airline course start date.

In the US, the process typically takes around three to nine months. For comparison, for those starting from scratch in the UK, it typically takes three to over eight years for a pilot to fly with a major airline. It's between two and over six years in the United States, depending on various factors.

Sources indicate that according to Planespotters.net, Virgin Atlantic right now operates an all-widebody fleet of 44 aircraft with an average age of 8.4 years. These include 14 Airbus A330s (six A330-300s and nine A330neos), 12 Airbus A350-1000s, and 17 Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. This makes it one of the largest all-widebody fleets in the world, although, for comparison, this total would only represent around 15% of Emirates' giant all-widebody fleet.

Virgin Atlantic's outstanding A330-900 orders will replace its remaining fleet of legacy A330-300s by 2027 while growing the overall fleet. The airline was established in 1984 and serves around 29 destinations, mostly from its hubs at London Heathrow and Manchester. The airline is also a member of SkyTeam and is 49% owned by Delta Air Lines. Virgin Atlantic has evolved into a mixed network carrier that serves both leisure-heavy destinations and business-heavy routes.

According to recent reports, it offers flights to Caribbean destinations like Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Grenada, Jamaica (Montego Bay), Mexico's Cancun, St. Lucia, and St. Vincent and the Grenadines. Its US destinations include Las Vegas, Orlando, Miami, Tampa, as well as some other less leisure-heavy destinations, such as Boston. Virgin has flights on some other non-leisure routes, including to India and Nigeria.

Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
  • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.
  • Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., mentioned he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday revealed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

According to recent reports, “I think it’s outrageous,” remarked Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”.

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he noted.

In a recent development, there is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson stated Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

In a recent development, sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

In a recent development, A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a strategy in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle remarked they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability matter, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” stated Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-fresh business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet at the moment consists of 25 planes, including:.

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The proposal is for the 787-9s to get all-latest cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats right now on the planes).

In a recent development, the 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

Industry observers note that we’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

According to recent reports, the plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Right now, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Industry observers note that seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s newly introduced Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

Sources indicate that aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's newly introduced premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the upcoming Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a new product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

Aeromexico is planning some significant upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service issues at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a new initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

In a recent development, emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a latest initiative involving this small group of employees:.

On 3 November, Emirates introduced a new initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

It goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

Industry observers note that when it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

According to recent reports, I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

Recent findings suggest that anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

It has been revealed that emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

Bilt is the platform known for providing rewards for housing payments. Earlier this year we saw massive changes at Bilt, including an overhaul of the credit card portfolio, plus fresh ways that housing rewards are offered.

Recent findings suggest that there are many innovative things about Bilt, including that there’s a Bilt Rent Day promotion on the first day of each month. With a upcoming month being right around the corner, I’d like to cover the details of the December 2026 Bilt Rent Day offer, as it includes both a JetBlue Mosaic elite status challenge, as well as an up to 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions (which isn’t a very good deal). It’s interesting to see a second month in a row with no transfer bonus….

There are a couple of aspects to the Bilt Rent Day promotion, including the ability to earn bonus points (which is the same every month), plus at least one additional promotion.

Note that Bilt Rent Day promotions are generally valid from 12:00AM ET until 11:59PM PT, so technically you have around 27 hours to take advantage of them.

It has been revealed that bilt has a portfolio of credit cards, including the no annual fee Bilt Blue Card (learn more), $95 annual fee Bilt Obsidian Card (learn more), and $495 annual fee Bilt Palladium Card (learn more) (Rates & Fees). Personally, I think the Bilt Palladium Card is by far the most lucrative.

It has been revealed that on the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

In a recent development, on December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a bonus when members redeem points for statement credits. The bonus you’re eligible for depends on which Bilt credit card you have, as follows:.

According to recent reports, let me cut to the chase — don’t redeem your points this way. It’s a bad value. Ordinarily you get 0.55 cents per Bilt point for statement credit redemptions, so even with a 100% bonus, you’re looking at getting 1.1 cents per point. Hard pass.

On December 1, 2026, Bilt is offering a JetBlue TrueBlue Mosaic status match challenge, and the status you’re eligible for depends on your Bilt elite status, as follows:.

Sources indicate that the status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:.

Sources indicate that regardless of which tier you initially match to, the status you get to keep is based on the activity over the course of those three months. As a reminder, you earn one tile for every $100 spent on JetBlue, or every $1,000 spent on a co-branded JetBlue credit card. So renewing status requires anywhere from $1,000 to $4,000 of airfare spending, or $10,000 to $40,000 of credit card spending.

This of course comes at a generally useful time for JetBlue elite status, given that the airline is introducing first class, with space available upgrades being an elite perk. However, it’s worth emphasizing that this really isn’t such a special offer, as it’s basically just JetBlue’s standard status match challenge offer. Except in this case, you can unlock it with Bilt elite status rather than airline elite status.

According to recent reports, on the first day of each month, Bilt offers a Rent Day promotion. In addition to earning up to double points for purchases, for December 2026, there are two offers members can take advantage of.

One offer is for up to a 100% bonus on statement credit redemptions, which can get you at most 1.1 cents per point of value. Please don’t redeem your points that way. JetBlue is also offering a status match challenge, whereby Bilt members can receive Mosaic 1 or Mosaic 2 status for a period of 90 days, and can then extend status through early 2028, with the opportunity to earn up to Mosaic 3 status, based on how many tiles are earned.

Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
  • However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

However, I swiftly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

Sources indicate that as the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and indicated the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically said, “that means nothing.”.

Sources indicate that so they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

According to recent reports, once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

Recent findings suggest that only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a substantial deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

Airline loyalty is really notable to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

Recent findings suggest that that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That noted, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

Even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

It was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

It has been revealed that as for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

Imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

It’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of newly introduced Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

According to recent reports, if I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….

Recent findings suggest that the British first edition of The Managerial Revolution that I picked up in a Charing Cross Road shop a quarter century ago tells us much about the work itself. I’ve read it four times, conscripted it as an airplane companion, and brought it to the beach. Yet its binding remains strong, its cover quite flexible, and its pages yellowing but intact. We no longer much refer to let alone read such 1941 bestsellers as Clifton Fadiman’s Reading I’ve Liked or Margaret Leech’s Reveille in Washington. But James Burnham, much like my strong and solid copy of his most famous book, endures.

Recent findings suggest that burnham, who entered the world 121 years ago Sunday and left it nearly 40 years ago, very much remains part of the Great Conversation. The Managerial Revolution, anticipating as it did the ascension of technocrats, specialists, and the bureaucratic elite as a sort of ruling class, surely helped in that regard. Burnham remains read, despite no Burnhamite clique in academia or organized faction among movement conservatives dedicated to advancing his ideas. Kirkians, Straussians, and Randians exist. Why no James Burnham Preservation Society with an accompanying secret handshake?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore.
  • As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.
  • Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, american Airlines has just officially “retired” its Flagship First product on the Boeing 777-300ER, meaning that no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore. The good news is that an updated business class product is in the process of being rolled out, and that’s something that should benefit a lot of travelers.

As I’ve covered in the past, American is in the process of eliminating its “premium” first class product, and that change was just implemented for flights as of this week on the carrier’s biggest planes.

Specifically, the Boeing 777-300ER is American’s “flagship” aircraft, with 20 of the planes in the fleet. As of this week, the airline is no longer selling first class on these planes. Now, plenty of 777-300ERs with these cabins are still flying around, as American has just started reconfiguring its 777-300ERs with latest cabins, including the new business class.

Recent findings suggest that still, for flights effective immediately, first class seats are just being sold as standard business class seats, and any business class passenger can select seats in the first two rows (you’d think they’d try to charge extra or at least reserve them for select elite members, but nope). So there will no longer be a differentiated soft product… not that there was much of a difference as of late anyway!

With this change, no US carrier offers an international first class product anymore either, so it very much is the end of an era. American’s 777 first class seats were controversial — on the one hand, I kind of love how they swivel, though on the other hand, they really lack privacy, and the soft product left a lot to be desired.

I expect we’ll continue to see these planes flying around well into late 2027, or possibly even into 2028, depending on how fast the retrofit project happens. American’s dedicated first class ground product has also largely been discontinued, as Flagship First Dining has turned into Flagship Dining, so a la carte lounge dining is now available to eligible business class passengers as well.

It’s great that these planes will be getting fresh business class suites, as they’ll also be the aircraft belonging to a US carrier with the most business class seats, as they’ll have 70 of them… that’s lot!

While American has now eliminated its international first class product, it’s worth emphasizing that the airline still technically has a “premium” first class, in the sense of a cabin above business class.

Recent findings suggest that specifically, American still has its specially configured Airbus A321T aircraft, which are used primarily for flights between Fresh York (JFK) and Los Angeles (LAX) and San Francisco (SFO). The planes have 10 reverse herringbone seats spread across five rows, in a 1-1 configuration.

American also looks to eliminate this product, as the A321Ts will be reconfigured into standard A321 domestic configuration aircraft, and A321XLRs will be taking over the transcon routes.

American has stopped selling first class on these planes for flights as of March 28, 2027. After that date we’ll still see some of the planes flying with the cabins, but the first class seats will simply be sold as business class.

According to recent reports, american Airlines has officially eliminated its international first class product, as Boeing 777-300ERs no longer have Flagship First for sale. These planes are being retrofitted, as first class seats are being eliminated, and newly introduced business class suites are being introduced. However, the planes will keep flying around with the current cabins for quite some time, and business class passengers can freely assign the first class seats.

In the spring, we’ll see American eliminate its last “premium” first class product, which is the A321T first class cabin, as those planes are replaced by A321XLRs.

    I just got back to Rio after a quick trip to Ireland for Aer Lingus’ event to showcase their upcoming A330 cabins, including its first-ever premium economy.

    I flew Air France economy both ways, and I’m glad I resisted the offer of $420 during online check-in to upgrade the outbound overnight economy leg. Ironically, it was the long day-flight back where I actually wished I’d upgraded.

    It has been revealed that however, to answer the economy vs. premium economy question, it all comes down to maximising comfort, and I think this is easier to do in economy than premium economy.

    If, like me, sleeping upright or on your back is almost impossible, then what follows will likely apply to you.

    The main reason I’m deterred to pick premium economy for overnight flights is because of the fixed armrests, where tray tables are sometimes stowed in this cabin.

    Despite the extra recline and leg rest element (which sometimes makes it even harder to get comfortable), the fixed armrests restrict the ability to sleep any way other than straight like a pencil.

    To make matters worse, they stop you from lying across more than one seat if you find yourself in an empty row.

    In a recent development, it’s for that reason that I much prefer economy. While having a row to yourself isn’t guaranteed, there’s at least a chance of being able to move around the cabin, or stretch out into an empty seat. No matter where you sit or how empty the cabin is, you can’t do that in premium economy.

    Another element of my pre-trip planning that I expect many of you to relate to is the fact it takes me so long umming and aahing over the best seat to pick.

    Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status (SkyTeam Elite Plus), I could pick any seat in the economy cabin of the Boeing 777-200ER for free from 72 hours before departure.

    In a recent development, I narrowed it down to an empty seat in the exit row, and the only row of three with an empty middle seat. I didn’t even consider one of the many empty middle rows of four seats in case they filled up before take off and I ended up in an aisle with no window to rest my head. Using the window or plane’s fuselage to rest my head on is the only saving grace for me when trying to sleep sitting upright.

    As the empty exit seat would have the same restricting fixed partition as premium, I decided against that, too.

    Recent findings suggest that after the “boarding complete” announcement was made, the middle seat in my row remained empty, and there were three seats free in the middle of row 25, a row in front. I explained to the girl in the aisle seat that if one of us moved to the other row, we’d both have three seats to ourselves. She didn’t seem to understand my point, and remarked she’d prefer to sit in the aisle than us both have three free seats to ourselves.

    I didn’t want to move to the middle seats either, so I got as comfortable as I could using the middle seat and the pillow I brought from home.

    Recent findings suggest that in the end, I did manage to get some half decent curled up shut eye (the thick pillow protected my back from the hard parts of the seat when propped against the fuselage). However, when I went to the loo, I noticed some people in the rear cabin had got lucky and were fast asleep spread across a whole four seats.

    Maybe I’ll take more of a risk next time….

    Sources indicate that I’m not saying economy is always a better choice than premium. For example, I’d always recommend Emirates’ pretty darn impressive premium economy over economy, because it genuinely is several steps up from economy.

    If it was up to me, I’d have had a lie-flat seat for the overnight segment. I didn’t, and I’m pretty certain I got better sleep quality curled up across two seats in economy that I would have almost upright on my back in premium.

    Would you ever choose economy over premium economy?

While I am beyond lucky with paid work travel and other factors not to have flown back-of-the-bus economy (or PE) for a very long time, I think this reviews adds an excellent perspective on air travel options, trade offs with hard and soft product in different classes of service, and seat design. Airlines don’t think about these in isolation one service class to another, so why should we? Also, the comments about sleeping position and comfort apply in any class of service (looking at you, SQ). Lots of food for thought about travel options.

    Recent findings suggest that there's another viable strategy for flying long-haul economy that I read about in some book - so booze, and then some more booze, and then a bit more booze. In essence, the idea is you don't pull the brakes on booze until the economy chair rivals and beats La Premiere. Just what I read in some book...

    It has been revealed that I had one of my longest inflight sleeps of 8 hours in an exit row economy window seat. As a terrible plane sleeper that was incredible so I will stick with that as the best place to sleep if I am not in J.

    I always prefer an economy window exit seat over premium econ. At 6’ 2 I find the leg rests in Premium highly uncomfortable too… much prefer to bring my bag down after take off in econ and use as a foot rest.     Recent findings suggest that I think I’ll have to disagree. There’s also the fact that you have to be either very lucky or well informed of a flights load factor patterns to be guaranteed to snag multiple seats in a row, and the fact that there will be other passengers looking to do the same thing. I sleep just fine in high speed rail second class seats which based purely on measurements seem comparable to premium economy , so I imagine I’d be plenty comfortable in a premium economy seat too.

    #42534. Latest Update: Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1240 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1240 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Sources indicate that trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he launched a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    In a recent development, “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump mentioned as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    Industry observers note that “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Upcoming York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    Industry observers note that “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump stated, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    According to recent reports, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of concerns, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer mentioned.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    Sources indicate that nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He mentioned it was “crucial” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers stated they doubted very much would come from it.

    “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    According to recent reports, “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal said Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    On spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to quickly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    Sources indicate that john M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.
