    In a recent development, in the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week declared latest export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors. These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. The new interim rules target three vulnerabilities: Chinese rerouting of U.S.-made AI chips through third countries, rented access to AI computing power, and Chinese chip designers’ ability to manufacture advanced chips at non-Chinese facilities.

    It has been revealed that the Nvidia scandal—including the alleged rerouting of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China and the Trump administration’s apparent quiescence—underscores the scope of the Chinese threat to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The latest rules close crucial gaps, but they do not resolve the threat. The next area where the United States is especially exposed is the Gulf, where the most advanced U.S. chips are now arriving, to be utilized in data centers operated by partners that maintain extensive ties with China.

    According to recent reports, the Gulf magnifies the Nvidia problem. Both the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are trying to shift their economies away from oil, and they’re placing AI at the center of their strategies. In May 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that both countries would be able to purchase advanced U.S. chips to help facilitate these efforts. Abu Dhabi and Riyadh are financing massive AI buildouts, where Nvidia chips will be installed, operated, and even rented to customers or cloud tenants. The two monarchies are taking advantage of their desert land areas, access to lower-cost energy, and deep coffers, offering Nvidia an appealing market and affording Washington an opportunity to keep U.S. technology at the center of the AI buildout.

    Sources indicate that both the Saudis and the Emiratis, however, also maintain deep relations with China. Washington fears that Beijing could gain access, intentional or not, through its contractors or cloud customers—or via hardware or software that may be connected to U.S. systems or chips. Chinese infiltration could occur through a trusted partner, with or without their knowledge, without directly acquiring the restricted chips.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s why companies such as the UAE’s Group 42 have caught the eye of China watchers and technology hawks. The group’s past links to China and its tech sector, even though the company publicly renounced them after the Biden administration declared it a security risk, raise questions that diplomatic assurances cannot resolve. The problem is not what the company indicates but whether its operations, ownership, partnerships, and access to sensitive technology can be independently verified and insulated from possible Chinese exploitation.

    Saudi Arabia presents a similar challenge. The kingdom is pursuing AI autonomy by seeking control over every layer of the technology stack. But Washington will want evidence that Saudi officials can protect their data centers and cloud services from unauthorized access. And that case is increasingly difficult to make as Saudi Arabia continues to partner with both U.S. and Chinese technology companies.

    The new rules make the Gulf an notable litmus test for whether Washington can enforce its new approach in third-country data centers. Gulf-based facilities will need to prevent restricted consumers from accessing compute power enabled by U.S. chips, including indirectly through the cloud or other intermediaries. It’s not just about whether a Chinese manufacturer or user can rent compute power through a Gulf partner, but also whether the safeguards are in place for partners who maintain U.S. compute power to verify ownership and the affiliations of users.

    U.S. export controls were designed for trade in tangible goods, but the Commerce Department has now acknowledged that simply controlling the physical movement of chips is not enough. The newly introduced rules extend export controls to some forms of remote access and computing power—intended, for example, to prevent a Chinese organization from renting access to a processor through a data center or cloud provider. The new rule is a major step forward but not a complete solution. Safeguarding U.S. chips will require more than protecting the physical product or regulating direct access. It will require oversight of the people and systems that can use the computing power that those chips provide. That means guarding not just the chips’ physical location but also their ownership, network architecture, and consumer access.

    It has been revealed that instead of determining which country or firm is purchasing a chip, an export policy will need to ask who will own and operate the facility, who can administer the compute power, which customers can rent its processors, what the networking and software infrastructure is made of, the nationality of people, and even whether the systems can be accessed outside of where they are housed. A processor being utilized in a Gulf data center, for example, may be used to provide computing power to a restricted Chinese company or state institution through the cloud—so controls must follow the user, not just the export.

    Industry observers note that nvidia sells the most advanced chips in the business. Its former CEO, who made himself the face of the manufacturer’s strategy and government relations, was close with Trump and has decried more stringent export controls on AI chips, arguing that such restrictions will merely move more consumers toward Chinese suppliers like Huawei. His influence may have helped persuade Trump to sell limited amounts of the H200 chip to China. But the concern extends beyond Huang’s influence. Questions about the administration’s handling of the policy—including conflicts of interest involving U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s own financial interests in Nvidia, and other relationships between U.S. officials and companies that may have benefited from certain sales, like Jared Kushner’s—warrant a review of these decisions. Regulators should begin by reexamining the decision to allow the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

    A fresh oversight policy would not entail a crackdown on Nvidia or a blanket ban on selling further advanced chips to Gulf states. Instead, Washington would expand access only when Gulf states meet specific conditions and establish guidelines for continuously evaluating who can access the technology. The new framework should become the baseline for future Gulf licenses that can identify approved facilities and consumers; limit chip quantities and aggregate compute power; prohibit restricted access and rentals; and require oversight of inventories, access logs, and control standards. Washington should also retain the right to suspend a license at any time. China has already sought to lease capacity through data centers in Europe and accessed U.S. chips to train its models through systems in Thailand.

    When the Democrats take control of the U.S. Congress in January, they will likely press for tougher oversight of foreign chip deals—as they should. Democrats and Republicans have a considerable opportunity to work together on this issue. Even though this week’s new rules help address some of the areas of concern, they are an executive branch policy and thus subject to change at any moment. Congress can focus on passing the Remote Access Security Act, which will require export policy to include remote access controls, and the AI Overwatch Act, which will give Congress more oversight over foreign chip sales.

    Industry observers note that for the UAE and Saudi Arabia, access to the most advanced chips is still possible but now comes with stronger U.S. demands—and any failure to adhere to those conditions should mean that access is immediately cut off. Fair or not, the Nvidia scandal raises the cost of assuming that trust is enough protection.

    However, tighter U.S. restrictions also carry some risk. If U.S. requirements become too stringent, intrusive, costly, or unpredictable, Gulf governments may turn back toward Chinese tech or tilt toward other suppliers with fewer restrictions. Greater reliance on Chinese tech would not replace the U.S. technological edge overnight but over the long term, it could well reduce U.S. influence.

    According to recent reports, the UAE and Saudi Arabia are seeking slightly different things. The UAE is leading the space in dealmaking and pushing the next generation of AI models, while Saudi Arabia is seeking to build out local compute capacity. For both, ongoing relationships with Chinese tech companies will remain an issue, and Washington will need stringent controls and verifications on who can access and use the systems.

    According to recent reports, china’s challenge to U.S. AI is a serious threat, and the United States must strengthen its technological defenses in the Gulf and elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s newly introduced rules are a meaningful step in closing the regulatory gap in U.S. export policy on chips. The Saudis’ and Emiratis’ AI ambitions make them key tests of whether the United States can enforce this approach. That requires systematic and continuous scrutiny of many more layers of the AI value chain than current U.S. export controls offer, including ownership, users, infrastructure, and remote access. The Saudis and Emiratis will, of course, say that they can be trusted. But in the post-Huang AI space, it is simply too risky to rely on assurances alone.

    #42392. Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3531 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    Trump Is Facing a Very Different North Korea

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3531 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021.
    • EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.
    • Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    STEPHEN E. BIEGUN was Deputy Secretary of State from December 2019 to January 2021 and Special Representative for North Korea from 2018 to 2021. He is a Distinguished Fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    EMMA CHANLETT-AVERY is Senior Director for Political-Security Affairs and Deputy Director of the Washington office of the Asia Society Policy Institute.

    And Now He Needs a Newly introduced Strategy.

    In a recent development, stephen E. Biegun and Emma Chanlett-Avery.

    Donald Trump has Pyongyang on his mind. In recent months, the U.S. president has made comments to the media suggesting he is in communication with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. In an August 17 Truth Social post, for instance, Trump announced that the United States would scale back joint military drills with South Korea. The decision, he wrote, was “based on my very good relationship with Kim Jong Un,” describing the dictator as “unthreatening and respectful.”.

    According to recent reports, trump has not been subtle about his desire to restart diplomacy with Kim. With an eye on his legacy and the war with Iran stalemated, he is eager to notch a foreign policy win. During his first term, Trump held two historic U.S.–North Korean summits aimed at denuclearizing the Korean Peninsula—but both foundered because of the countries’ disparate expectations for the terms of a deal. Since his reelection, Trump has been looking to reopen talks with Kim. The ball is now in Pyongyang’s court, and Kim has signaled, if not an eagerness for renewed engagement, at least an unwillingness to rule it out. In August, after Trump insisted for the second time that he was in touch with Pyongyang, Kim Yo Jong—the leader’s influential sister—released a statement that read: “Regarding the reports from Washington about recent communication between the top leaders of North Korea and the U.S., I am completely unaware of such matters. It has been stated on numerous occasions that our head of state holds fond personal memories and positive feelings toward Trump. The relationship between the leaders remains excellent.” Although this is far from an agreement to meet, Kim Jong Un is not closing the door.

    If leader-to-leader talks materialize, Trump may believe his personal rapport with Kim will yield a deal. But he will be facing a very different North Korea than the one at their last meeting in 2019. The fallout from unfinished diplomacy during Trump’s first term, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global trends such as the sharp escalation in U.S.-Chinese strategic rivalry and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have destabilized the security landscape and created formidable obstacles to peaceful engagement. Meanwhile, North Korea’s continued nuclear and conventional military expansion and the growing support it is receiving from Moscow have strengthened Kim’s hand. Facing an emboldened Pyongyang, Trump can no longer fall back on the same concessions and negotiation tactics he used in previous talks.

    Industry observers note that for a U.S.–North Korean summit to be successful, the United States must approach it with well-defined strategic goals and a clear understanding of what concessions it is willing to make. Washington should shift its focus away from denuclearization, at least in the short term, to concentrate on more achievable nuclear arms control and safety measures. The United States should also maintain a capable troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and reiterate its security assurances—particularly its nuclear-deterrence guarantees—to regional allies such as South Korea and Japan.

    Recent findings suggest that although diplomacy with North Korea has historically been difficult, Trump is eager to meet with Kim, and both sides want to avoid pushing the Indo-Pacific toward nuclear proliferation or all-out war. Careful engagement with Pyongyang could defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula and lay the groundwork for a more stable security landscape.

    It has been revealed that since the U.S.–North Korean summit in 2019, the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have reshaped the Indo-Pacific in ways that strengthen Kim’s hand. The U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has drawn Washington’s focus away from Asia as, for the third time in the past quarter century, U.S. strategic attention and military assets have surged to the Middle East. The last American aircraft carrier stationed in the Indo-Pacific departed for the Persian Gulf in August, and U.S. strikes on Iran have rapidly depleted American munitions stockpiles. Washington’s Indo-Pacific allies, already strained by Trump’s abrupt policy shifts and punishing tariffs, are now concerned about deteriorating deterrence. Asian economies—many of which are deeply dependent on Middle Eastern energy supplies—have contracted as the Strait of Hormuz has remained compromised. Amid signs of further American retrenchment, U.S. allies and partners are increasingly skeptical about Washington’s commitment to the region.

    Even more consequential is Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which has benefited North Korea in numerous ways. Moscow and Pyongyang’s once dormant relationship has flourished as Kim has sent thousands of munitions to replenish Russia’s depleted stockpiles and thousands of soldiers to fight and die in the ongoing ground war. Images of the newly introduced memorial to the Korean People’s Army soldiers who have perished in the invasion suggest an already significant loss of North Korean lives. In return, Pyongyang has received generous assistance from Moscow in violation of international sanctions, including abundant financial support for Kim’s regime and technology transfers that have enhanced North Korean military capabilities and may help Pyongyang more accurately deliver intercontinental ballistic missiles aimed at the United States. Russian patronage allows Kim to shower his regime’s elites with the economic benefits needed to cement their loyalty.

    Still, it is worth questioning how durable this partnership is. After more than four years of grinding warfare with no end in sight, Moscow is increasingly isolated and may be in a poor position to continue supporting Pyongyang. Russia’s preoccupation with Ukraine has allowed China to expand its presence in Central Asia, for instance, and Turkey to deepen its influence in Azerbaijan. Russian aggression has spurred Armenia and Moldova to look westward, and hundreds of thousands of young Russian men have fled the country to avoid military conscription while over a thousand Western companies have left. International sanctions are starving Russia of badly needed capital and technology, and Russian war policies have created huge imbalances and inflation, possibly with worse to come for the Russian economy. If North Korea continues to actively support Moscow in this war, and Russia fails or is defeated, the world will become a much more hostile place for Pyongyang.

    Sources indicate that russia and North Korea’s deepening ties have already begun to reshape China’s interests in the region. Beijing is still Pyongyang’s most important partner, but the dynamic has changed considerably in recent years. Beijing previously saw denuclearization as a top priority on the Korean Peninsula—a shared objective, and at times a rare area of cooperation, with the United States. It disliked the destabilizing impact that North Korea’s pursuit of nuclear weapons had on tensions between the North and South and expended political capital responding to international condemnation of Pyongyang. Between 2006 and 2017, Beijing agreed to a series of UN Security Council resolutions that imposed sanctions and other restrictions on Pyongyang in response to six North Korean nuclear tests. Now, pressed to maintain its influence in Pyongyang amid a growing Russian–North Korean security relationship—and with the rest of the world distracted by other geopolitical crises—China has gone silent on the matter. When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited North Korea in June to reassert his influence, denuclearization was not publicly mentioned. China’s fresh approach will make U.S. engagement on this issue more challenging and risks driving other regional powers, such as South Korea and Japan, to reconsider their own policies on the deployment or development of nuclear weapons.

    Industry observers note that whether Pyongyang reengages with the United States may also depend on how much North Korea relies on China for economic support. Much of North Korean commerce passes through China, and although Beijing and Pyongyang’s relationship appears fairly stable, it remains wary and transactional, with each side skeptical of the other’s motives. North Korea may seek to reengage with the United States to counterbalance its overdependence on China, or as a hedge against Russia’s failure in its war with Ukraine. Conversely, as Trump and Xi upgrade and stabilize U.S.-Chinese relations, China could step in to broker the next Trump-Kim meeting.

    The Kim dynasty has long vexed U.S. policymakers. Washington has sought multiple deals with North Korea, including during Trump’s first-term summits with Kim, but missteps and mistrust on both sides derailed them. Pyongyang has proved resilient to both U.S. and international sanctions. Indeed, during the COVID-19 pandemic, North Korea sealed its borders and deprived itself far more severely than sanctions could, yet it still survived. U.S. congressional interventions on human rights and humanitarian aid, meanwhile, have mostly failed to change North Korea’s behavior. Pyongyang has also cushioned the impact of sanctions by engaging in cybertheft, such as its $6.3 billion heist against the cryptocurrency exchange Binance this October. All the while, Pyongyang has steadily advanced its military capabilities and expanded its nuclear arsenal.

    According to recent reports, although Washington’s previous attempts to rein in North Korea have failed, Trump’s renewed eagerness to meet with Kim and his unorthodox approach to foreign policy could provide a upcoming opening for diplomacy. Trump has cultivated a direct relationship with Kim, shunning the bureaucratic negotiations that usually precede a deal. While a performative summit alone would be of little benefit to U.S. interests, Washington could use reengagement with Pyongyang to thaw inter-Korean relations and stabilize the peninsula by slowing or freezing North Korea’s nuclear buildup. Those goals may seem conventional, but as regional tensions worsen and Pyongyang’s nuclear arsenal grows, they are essential to averting potentially catastrophic conflict.

    Recent findings suggest that three questions cast a shadow over the possibility of renewed engagement between the United States and North Korea. First is the specific purpose of restarting engagement: What is the goal? Second is how to reopen communications. Despite Trump’s claims, there is no real proof that he has recently interacted with Kim. All evidence suggests the last contact between American and North Korean officials was in 2019, and it may be challenging to break a seven-year drought. Third is what are the incentives and tradeoffs the United States would be willing to consider as part of a negotiation—the same matter that bedeviled U.S. and North Korean officials in Hanoi.

    Sources indicate that one possible formula for progress is focusing, at least temporarily, on steady arms control and international safety controls rather than the elusive goal of denuclearization. Denuclearization should remain Washington’s ultimate aspiration. But in the meantime, a North Korea awash with even more nuclear weapons makes the world only more dangerous. This approach will require serious diplomacy to minimize second-order consequences, particularly to avoid weakening U.S. alliances in the Indo-Pacific or triggering a collapse of the nuclear nonproliferation regime among nations that might see their only recourse as acquiring their own nuclear weapons. China, and perhaps even Russia, may concur with Washington on this point, and a shared desire to avoid more nuclear states in East Asia could help restart engagement.

    Kim has substantially more leverage now than in earlier encounters with Trump. Reopening communication will require using a mix of positive and negative assurances to convince him that he is unlikely to get a better chance to strike a deal. Kim may press the United States to scale back aspects of its cooperation with South Korea—such as joint military exercises and support for Seoul’s pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines—as preconditions for a meeting with Trump. Kim may even propose his own assurances of peace on the peninsula in exchange for a reduction of U.S. military forces in South Korea, although it is unclear whether Trump would agree to such conditions.

    In the worst-case scenario, Kim may take advantage of Trump’s eagerness to make a deal to extract weighty concessions from the United States. Kim has little reason to meet with Trump now, unless he calculates that he can secure major terms such as de facto recognition as a nuclear state, reduced sanctions, or a complete withdrawal of U.S. troops from the peninsula. Kim would likely insist that there be no discussion of denuclearization, North Korea’s support for the invasion of Ukraine, Pyongyang’s human rights abuses, or a final accounting for Japanese citizens kidnapped by North Korea under the rule of Kim Il Sung. Granting such concessions would end the U.S.–South Korean alliance.

    Recent findings suggest that to ensure North Korea does not exploit the Trump administration, Washington must carefully consider what tradeoffs it is willing to make. Lifting sanctions, abandoning or delaying the denuclearization process, temporarily accepting North Korea as a nuclear state, and reducing the U.S. military presence in South Korea are all long-standing demands of Kim’s regime that are likely on the table. Although lifting international sanctions would require UN Security Council consensus, Trump may be willing to reduce unilateral U.S. sanctions, which he considers an obstacle to better bilateral relations and which have been ineffective in stemming Pyongyang’s nuclear advances.

    It has been revealed that although denuclearization has been a major talking point for U.S. administrations since the early 1990s, the Trump administration may need to set it aside, at least in the short term. Pyongyang’s nuclear capabilities have increased since Trump’s 2018 and 2019 summits with Kim, suggesting that the stalemate caused by continued U.S. demands for the full-scale dismantlement of North Korea’s nuclear program may have given Kim time and space to grow his arsenal. Even if denuclearization remains a long-term U.S. priority—and it should—pragmatism is essential to reducing the threat posed by Kim’s regime. In exchange for stepping away from denuclearization, Trump should demand that Kim freeze any further expansion of his arsenal and explore possibilities for greater strategic stability, including renewed inter-Korean dialogue, transparency and confidence-building efforts, security measures that bolster nuclear facilities’ safety and guard against accidents, and strict adherence to nonproliferation. Trump must make it clear to Kim that an unconstrained expansion of North Korea’s nuclear arsenal will pressure South Korea and Japan to deploy nuclear weapons on their territory and possibly develop their own.

    Recent findings suggest that regardless of Kim’s demands, the United States must preserve its troop presence on the Korean Peninsula and continue joint military exercises with South Korea as long as the threat of North Korean aggression persists. The mantra of U.S. troops in South Korea is “ready to fight tonight.” Joint military exercises keep U.S. and South Korean forces prepared for combat, which is essential to deterring North Korean attacks. It would be dangerous and irresponsible to send American soldiers, sailors, marines, and airmen to the peninsula without ensuring peak readiness. Instead of withdrawing troops, the United States should offer confidence-building measures to North Korea—practices that reduce the risk of conflict breaking out because of misjudgment. These could include military-to-military engagement and security reassurances among the United States, South Korea, and North Korea, or greater transparency around military exercises—allowing observers on a reciprocal basis, for example. Sustaining Washington’s alliance with South Korea and avoiding cascading nuclear proliferation are critical to U.S. interests in the region. American negotiators must remind Kim that the U.S. military presence and its extended nuclear-deterrence guarantees for Seoul and Tokyo hold back even larger conventional military—and possibly nuclear—buildups in the region.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, North Korea and the United States—and perhaps, in time, South Korea and Japan—should sustain diplomatic engagement by agreeing to assign diplomats to each other’s capitals through reciprocal liaison offices, which would maintain relations without granting full diplomatic recognition. In 2018 and 2019, the two sides discussed housing such diplomats in the German Embassy in Pyongyang and the Swedish Embassy in Washington. Liaison offices would also stabilize and prolong the communication necessary to quietly work through complex negotiations.

    If North Korea rejects Trump’s overtures, the United States is not without options. Washington could pressure the Kim regime by intensifying the scale and tempo of joint military exercises with South Korea; deploying American armaments, including short-range ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and possibly nuclear weapons, to South Korea and Japan; and pursuing a new campaign to choke off North Korea’s economic resources through sanctions and interdiction. The United States could also deploy additional air defense assets to Japan and South Korea, including THAAD air defense radar systems and interceptors. Washington and its allies could dramatically expand efforts to undermine Kim’s rule by mounting sustained criticisms of North Korea’s dangerously large nuclear weapons arsenal and its use of international criminal enterprise to steal from and economically defraud other nations, which could spur other countries to curb their material or diplomatic support for North Korea or more aggressively sanction Kim’s regime.

    Beyond short-term negotiations, a fourth question is less complicated but just as important: What role should Japan and South Korea play in U.S. engagements with North Korea? Many past administrations, both Republican and Democratic, have considered coordination with allies essential to establishing a durable solution on the Korean Peninsula. But Trump’s antipathy toward alliances suggests close consultation with South Korea and Japan is unlikely. Their absence from the negotiating table may actually accelerate U.S.–North Korean engagement, because coordination across allied governments can be unwieldy and slow, and Pyongyang has not been receptive to past overtures by Seoul and Tokyo. Although South Korean President Lee Jae-myung and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi both rhetorically back engagement with North Korea, Pyongyang has bluntly rejected their outreach.

    Even if Seoul and Tokyo are not directly engaged in U.S.–North Korean diplomacy, they would still likely welcome a U.S.-led deal with Kim if it protects their core security interests. But a deal with Kim that ignores American allies’ concerns would be dangerous. South Korea harbors an appetite to develop its own nuclear arsenal, particularly if it feels U.S. security protections are receding. Should Seoul move in that direction, Tokyo would almost certainly reconsider its own nonnuclear status, potentially igniting a nuclear arms race in Asia. Given North Korea’s long-standing hostility toward both Japan and South Korea, proliferation would destabilize the Indo-Pacific and leave the global nonproliferation regime in tatters.

    Industry observers note that any deal, even one that addresses Seoul’s and Tokyo’s core interests, will likely need to be paired with American security reassurances to allies’ governments and publics. Japan and South Korea must continue building their own conventional defense capabilities while the United States sustains its commitment to defending its Asian allies—especially extended nuclear deterrence. The United States must pursue delicate, nuanced diplomacy to avoid creating a stronger, legitimized North Korea; straining its alliances with Seoul and Tokyo; and debilitating the international nonproliferation regime.

    In a recent development, despite the risks of U.S.–North Korean engagement, the time may be ripe to break the diplomatic paralysis that has allowed Pyongyang to advance its military capabilities for so long. The last two years of Trump’s presidency—particularly his summitry calendar in late 2026—will bring him to Asia, potentially facilitating a meeting with Kim. Such a visit would present the best chance for the kind of performative, high-profile meeting that both Trump and Kim favor.

    It has been revealed that trump is the ultimate iconoclast in traditional great-power politics, as evidenced by his shifting relationships with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which could shape Washington’s engagement with Pyongyang. Still, there may be a way to leverage Trump’s affection for Kim, and Kim’s recent restraint in criticizing the United States, to outline a deal that arrests the growing threat of North Korean nuclear weapons.

    In a recent development, the bruising Republican defeat in the U.S. midterm elections could also change North Korea’s diplomatic calculus, especially because it suggests Trump’s political standing in the United States has faltered, and he may struggle to deliver the results Kim seeks. Trump may force the issue, however, and propose a meeting with Kim after the November Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Summit in Shenzhen, China. It would not be surprising for Trump to suggest that this meeting take place in Pyongyang, putting Kim on the spot. If leader-to-leader talks occur, both sides should remember the central lesson from Trump’s first-term summits: engagement without sufficient preparation and clearly defined goals is not enough to strengthen security and stability on the Korean Peninsula.

    Growing tensions in the Indo-Pacific raise the prospect of a much darker future, where conditions on the Korean Peninsula remain unchanged and Asia’s entanglements in European and Middle Eastern conflicts metastasize into a new world war—perhaps ignited in Taiwan, the South China Sea, or the Korean Peninsula. Even if no war breaks out, in just a few years the United States could find itself in a world where Asia’s five current nuclear states are joined by two, three, or more new players.

    Sources indicate that but this future is not inevitable. All the leaders engaged in North Korean security debates—from Lee and Takaichi to Xi and Putin—want to avoid such escalation. Even the North Koreans surely recognize this is the most dangerous path. This shared goal means diplomacy is still possible, despite formidable challenges. For all Trump’s idiosyncrasies, one should take his desire to peacefully end tensions on the Korean Peninsula at face value. He has made his intentions clear. What happens next is up to Chairman Kim.

    #42390. Industry News: Is This the Beginning of the End for Modi?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1998 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignpolicy ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Is This the Beginning of the End for Modi?

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, thousands took to the streets in Newly introduced Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud.
    • A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance.
    • Thousands took to the streets in Latest Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Get audio access with any FP subscription.

    According to recent reports, thousands took to the streets in Newly introduced Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud. Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

    A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

    Thousands took to the streets in Latest Delhi last month to protest irregularities in electoral rolls and alleged election fraud. Reports claimed that more than 130 million voters were deleted from electoral lists, in ways that would benefit Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). But will this anger in New Delhi spread to the rest of the country, weakening Modi’s 12-year hold on power, or will it simply fizzle out as time passes and other concerns become urgent?

    A lot depends on India’s opposition parties and whether they can keep up the momentum until elections in 2029 and offer a viable alternative to the people—but equally on how the populace rates Modi’s performance. Has he raised their standard of living? Is the opposition right in alleging that the BJP is systematically hollowing out Indian democracy? Increasingly, those questions are being answered in a way that makes it seem like Modi has peaked.

    Industry observers note that at a Diwali party last month, a young Indian researcher in her mid-20s warned me against attending a protest rally. “The police will pick you up,” she said, her eyes wide open. In a recent protest, the Delhi police had locked down major parts of the capital and cracked down on protesters. The police cut off the internet, shut down local trains in key areas, and detained thousands, including journalists. Even those hanging around weren’t spared. “Our lawyer friends who went to the protest site to help the protesters were also beaten up,” she said. “Because our friends were detained and beaten, now we fear we could be next. You could be next.”.

    According to recent reports, this is starkly different from India in 2011, when tens of thousands flocked to Jantar Mantar, a historical protest site near Delhi’s power center, for an anti-corruption demonstration. That protest paved the way for the Congress-led government’s defeat and Modi’s entry into national politics in 2014. Modi’s government, however, appears to have drawn a very different lesson about how to deal with protests.

    Sources indicate that BJP leaders suggested removing protesters because they inconvenienced passersby and businesses. That line was parroted relentlessly in TV studios. In my travels in and around Delhi, I found that message landed with certain people—mostly those who also believed the BJP’s insinuation, which came without any evidence, that protests in India were a foreign ploy to destabilize the country. Protests in India unfolded at the same time as in France and elsewhere in Europe, and this was portrayed as a sign of collaboration.

    However, there appears to be a pattern in how the current Indian government discredits and responds to protests. A few months ago, when Indian students marched against an exam paper leak and jobless growth, the same police thrashed the students, even firing pellet guns. Some TV anchors claimed the police were the victims.

    These are unusual scenes in India, a democratic country where the right to protest is guaranteed under the constitution. India won its independence through peaceful protests against the British.

    Industry observers note that on Nov. 1, despite the police’s reported highhandedness, thousands of people from different parts of the country gathered for the mega protest at an alternative and government-approved protest site. By noon, as I reached Connaught Place in central Delhi, Congress workers were marching on the streets and calling for the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. They accused Kumar of working to benefit the BJP.

    But Kumar’s role and the discrepancies in electoral rolls weren’t the only reasons that pushed people to protest. Three Gen Z protesters stood in a corner, two of them wearing masks to avoid being identified by the police. “They picked up people after the protests last time, from their homes,” remarked one of the masked boys. All three had joined the protests for very different reasons but the same cause—saving Indian democracy.

    It has been revealed that the masked boy recounted the story of how his friend, a child, was terrified for his mother’s security when Hindu-Muslim riots unfolded in Delhi early 2020. He blamed the BJP for instigating the riots. The young man standing to his left hailed from West Bengal and was furious that his grandparents, both octogenarians, were knocked off the voters list and denied the right to cast their ballot. “[The government] wanted to exclude a certain community, Bengali Muslims that they falsely say are Bangladeshis, but everyone was affected,” he said. “They are dividing us on the basis of religion; this is not okay.”.

    Sources indicate that mihika Omseema refused to cover up her face. She mentioned her parents supported her and that gave her the strength to reveal her identity and take part in protests. She said she joined to protest against growing Hindu-Muslim polarization, falling economic standards, exam paper leaks, and a whole host of other problems. In Delhi, some neighborhoods revealed a mood where parents might join their children—if not at the protest grounds, then at the ballot. A senior gentleman and an upper-caste Hindu said, “Modi will not win Delhi, no chance,” but he confessed that Modi still had many supporters in the country. An 80-kilometer ride to Meerut has been shortened from more than 3 hours to less than 2 hours via a new flyover completed under Modi’s government, which has also built several other key highways linking cities in western Uttar Pradesh. Meerut, for the first time, has a fast train that reaches Delhi in less than an hour and thus expands employment potential. (Uttar Pradesh has the maximum number of electoral constituencies and plays a decisive role in forming the government in Delhi. Although central elections are still more than two years away, the state itself will go to the polls next year.).

    In Meerut, I heard a different set of complaints against the BJP. Younger people acknowledged infrastructure development but said there was still no work. Only Muslims were worried about growing polarization; Hindus were more upset with slow economic growth and a demolition drive to bulldoze illegal shops and other structures. “Of course, this will affect the BJP in the elections; people are, we are, very angry with the government,” said Aditya Kumar, who sat on a stool in his emptied and recently destroyed shop in a market where rubble had still not been cleared. He sold nuts, bolts, and other construction material. “The structures were illegal, but there is no other employment, so what were we supposed to do?” he said, highlighting the lack of industry and compulsion to resort to small retail businesses.

    Sources indicate that “This is dictatorship,” remarked Kumar, a staunch Modi supporter until the demolition drive. “And no one raises our voice because the media doesn’t broadcast anything critical of Modi.”.

    About a dozen other upper-caste Hindus in the city who professed to be pro-Modi mentioned the BJP was unlikely to win Meerut even if it retains the state. That could change if there were credible opposition, but they did not see a match. Congress scion Rahul Gandhi marched alongside protesters and promised to seek justice for those wrongfully detained or beaten up. In Delhi, Gen Z protesters spoke in his favor. But in a state deeply divided along caste lines, despite being upper caste, he is still not seen as an alternative.

    Akash, a 26-year-old from Bulandshahr, mentioned that the BJP will return to power because it had ensured quick payment for sugarcane to farmers like his father. “There are also more roads and police stations,” he said, emphasizing improvement in law and order under the BJP government led by Modi acolyte Yogi Adityanath. He said that Indians like him would rate Modi on economic development over the protests in Delhi or the state of Indian democracy. But he also didn’t want to give up his own right to protest or question the government.

    “If the choice is between a better economy and democracy, I choose the economy, but if it is between the economy and my ability to question the government, then I choose democracy,” he mentioned.

    Industry observers note that like Meerut in Uttar Pradesh, in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, local factors were adding to a sense that all was not well under the Modi government. But here, too, the protests were not the reason that people said the government could change. “Farmers are not being paid on time,” Bhawani Singh, a tourist taxi driver, said. “Our children will never go and protest like those in Delhi. But we are upset about the Agnipath scheme and the shortening of military service,” he said, referring to government intends to cut down the length of service below the rank of officer to four years and retain only a quarter for a full term. “Most kids here want to join the army or the police,” he said. (The government appears to have noticed the grievance, announcing earlier this month that two more years of service could be offered and a second chance at joining longer-term,, for those who meet the selection criteria.).

    Local factors remain paramount for Indians deciding how Modi has fared in his third term. The protests have had some effect on their overall assessment—distancing those affected by other government policies, while many remain ambivalent or supportive. The weakening of institutions isn’t yet a factor in how they vote, but it has been registered, as former supporters say the media is largely pliable, and now the Election Commission is suspected of being subservient.

    Recent findings suggest that the fence-sitters are the upper-caste Hindus who form the backbone of the BJP’s voter base. And while many are still firmly behind the party and backing Hindu dominance, at least some appeared uncomfortable with a slide away from democracy. “He wants to be Putin,” an upper-caste Hindu remarked  . “Now with the delimitation bill, the BJP is trying to ensure it always has enough seats to keep them in power,” he added, referring to legislation that will come up for voting in parliament next month and intends to expand the number of seats based on population. The same exercise in Jammu and Kashmir, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said, helped the BJP.

    The recent protests are occurring in the middle of Modi’s current stint in office. He still has time to assuage concerns. But the opposition will also have a chance to highlight its case about the weakening of democratic institutions and the threat to Indian democracy. And just as a political wave pushed Modi into office 12 years ago, another one could be building that will eventually sweep him out.

    #42388. A New Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3105 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    A New Kind of Foreign Agent

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.
    • Industry observers note that foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding.
    • Like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    How AI Is Reshaping Influence Operations in America.

    Industry observers note that foreign governments have tried to influence the United States since its founding. President George Washington warned in his Farewell Address that “foreign influence is one of the most baneful foes of republican government.” The old methods have certainly not gone out of vogue; just this week Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman who U.S. officials believe was working for Chinese intelligence. But today, a upcoming type of foreign agent has arrived: Chinese artificial intelligence companies.

    Like the foreign agents of old, the models these companies sell may seem harmless—just a cheap tool for American businesses to use. But their makers train them to promote the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). American businesses are outsourcing more and more critical decisions to AI. If Washington does nothing, those businesses will hand over control to models whose objective is to promote a foreign government.

    Although U.S. policymakers now debate banning Chinese AI, the tried-and-true American solution is not censorship but disclosure. In 1938, Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Rather than outlaw propaganda, FARA allowed foreign agents to continue spreading it—as long as they registered with the government and disclosed whom they really worked for. Their communications also had to carry a conspicuous label naming their foreign sponsor.

    FARA’s wisdom has aged well over the decades. In recent years, the Justice Department has ordered the Russian state television network RT and the Chinese state media organizations Xinhua and CGTN to register as foreign agents and to label their content as such. Those who failed to register as foreign agents, such as Paul Manafort, President Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign chairman, and former U.S. Representative David Rivera of Florida, were sentenced to prison. (Trump pardoned Manafort in 2020.).

    In a recent development, today, rather than banning AI companies controlled by foreign governments, the United States should treat them as foreign agents under FARA. No latest statute is needed. Washington should simply enforce the one on the books. Of course, FARA is no silver bullet against all foreign influence, but it fits the shape of this problem. A handful of known Chinese companies, such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, build the models that American businesses increasingly let think and act for them. The Justice Department can reach every one of them.

    It has been revealed that democracy is strong enough to survive foreign influence but not invisible foreign influence. And to make sure the world does not subordinate its decision-making to Beijing, Washington and its allies must create an allied AI compact and then spread their own models far and wide.

    According to recent reports, american AI models, such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, are under no obligation to promote the U.S. government’s message. Ask Claude about Trump’s and President Joe Biden’s biggest failures or about the United States’ darkest chapters, and it will answer. Not so for Chinese AI models. When I asked the Chinese chatbot DeepSeek to “tell me about the CCP” in November, it answered that the party “is the vanguard of the Chinese working class, the Chinese people, and the Chinese nation. . . . The Party’s leadership is the most essential characteristic of socialism with Chinese characteristics and is the fundamental guarantee for China’s development and progress.” Such boosterish language appears by design.

    By law, Chinese AI models must never go against the Chinese government. Under the country’s 2023 regulations on generative AI, they must “uphold the Core Socialist Values” and may not engage in “harming the nation’s image” or “undermining national unity and social stability.” The Chinese government released a technical standard that laid out what these high-level declarations mean in practice: AI developers should have a list of at least 10,000 banned keywords, and their models must refuse to answer at least 95 percent of test questions the CCP finds objectionable. Developers must also scrub their training data of any history Beijing does not like. In short, the models must act as card-carrying members of the CCP.

    Sources indicate that that is why, as the U.S. Commerce Department’s AI evaluators found in 2025, DeepSeek pushes Chinese propaganda at far higher rates than American models do, even when run on American servers. Estonia’s Foreign Intelligence Service found that DeepSeek inserted praise of the Chinese state unprompted, and it concluded that China uses DeepSeek to instill “a distorted, self-serving world view in the Western information space.”.

    But these models are not just propaganda parrots—they are taught to “think” about how to promote Beijing’s perspective. Ask an AI model something complex, and it will “reason” for a while. As it thinks, it produces an internal monologue called its chain of thought. Users rarely see it. There, it decides which facts are relevant and which to discard, what advice to give, and what autonomous actions to take. Silicon Valley is terrified that these chains of thought will become corrupt—that models will start scheming and lying, becoming “misaligned.” But a different kind of corruption is already here.

    Although American models’ chains of thought usually focus on helping the user, China’s do something else: prioritize the party line. When researchers funded by Sweden’s Psychological Defense Agency looked at how Qwen, Alibaba’s flagship model, reasons about China, they found an internal checklist to keep the answer positive, avoid criticism, and focus on achievements. So when an American company asks a question on which Beijing has a view, a Chinese model may discard all evidence that points the other way. As the world delegates more research, writing, and decision-making to Chinese AI models, it risks infusing the CCP’s goals into every action taken.

    These models are also highly persuasive. In a study published last year in Nature, researchers had some 6,000 voters in the United States, Canada, and Poland chat with AI models that argued for a candidate. The study found that a single conversation shifted the preferences of opposition voters in Canada and Poland by about ten percentage points. AI persuades by flooding a user with confident and authoritative-sounding facts—statistics, historical claims, and the like.

    According to recent reports, chinese AI models also exhibit strange behaviors beyond the spreading of propaganda. In October, the Canadian AI manufacturer Cohere reported that during a security test, Alibaba’s Qwen tried to upload a file to a cloud server in Beijing, completely unprompted. The behavior was rare for Qwen, only observed once in testing, and Cohere mentioned it could not tell whether it was “deliberate or a leftover glitch from training.” A study by the cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike found that when customers asked DeepSeek to write code that mentions groups Beijing finds politically “sensitive,” such as Tibetans, Uyghurs, or the religious movement Falun Gong, the model became up to 50 percent more likely to write code with severe security flaws. CrowdStrike suggested that one possible cause is China’s rule that models adhere to “core socialist values.”.

    Recent findings suggest that despite these findings, Chinese AI is enormously popular. Last year, downloads of Chinese open-weight models—AI models that anyone can download from the Internet and run on their own hardware—surpassed those of American ones across the world. Developers have built more than 150,000 models on Alibaba’s Qwen alone. By September 2026, Chinese models handled up to 67 percent of traffic on OpenRouter, a popular AI marketplace, up from around ten percent in February.

    Sources indicate that american companies have embraced them. In March, a user discovered that Cursor, a popular coding tool, had built its new model by retraining Kimi, a model from the Chinese organization Moonshot AI. Airbnb, DoorDash, and the legal-services AI company Harvey use Chinese models as well. Many others likely do, too, in secret. The models are spreading even faster abroad, from Germany’s Siemens to Singapore’s national AI program to startups in Africa. The reason is simple economics: Chinese models are very cheap and very good.

    Sources indicate that although most American AI companies do not release open-weight models, most Chinese companies do. So an American firm must pay Anthropic for each use of its unmodifiable models, but it can download Kimi for free, retrain it however it wants, and pay only for the electricity and chips to run it. Kimi also runs on a firm’s own servers, whereas Claude runs on Anthropic’s. Even if a organization uses the most expensive DeepSeek model run on DeepSeek’s servers, it can produce the same amount of text as Anthropic’s top models at one-20th the cost.

    In terms of capabilities, the research group Epoch AI judges Chinese models to be only about seven months behind American ones. For the price, they get the job done. And Chinese companies are now building agentic AI systems to compete with Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex. In October, DeepSeek released an open-source prototype of its “Super-Agent” system.

    Although AI is a new technology, Chinese companies such as DeepSeek and Moonshot AI fit FARA’s text and history. The statute applies when a foreign principal is identified; in the case of Chinese AI models, it is the Chinese government and the CCP. The Justice Department would also have to show that the Chinese AI tech giant acts “at the order, request, or under the direction or control” of the principal. Chinese AI companies would qualify because they must promote CCP viewpoints and cooperate with the state’s intelligence agencies. They also receive subsidies, and party organizations are embedded in each company. This is the difference between Chinese AI and other foreign AI. For example, France’s public investment bank has a stake in the French AI company Mistral, but no French law requires Mistral to build its models to serve the French government.

    Industry observers note that beijing will surely respond that Washington, too, has tried to control American AI companies, such as through Trump’s July 2025 executive order against “woke AI.” But that order affects only what federal agencies can procure, and a manufacturer can opt out of being a federal contractor. Meanwhile, Chinese law forces Chinese AI companies to train their models to “support, assist, and cooperate with national intelligence efforts.”.

    Sources indicate that for FARA to apply, the agent must engage in certain activities, such as attempting to influence Americans or publishing content. Chinese AI companies do both by distributing models that spread propaganda. The statute exempts purely commercial activity, but only if it is “private and nonpolitical” and does not directly promote a foreign government’s political interests. Chinese AI models engage in political speech on a government’s behalf, and the Justice Department has denied the exemption to agents of foreign governments.

    Industry observers note that after registration, the genius of the statute can kick in. Chinese AI companies must disclose extensive information to the U.S. government: their funding sources, their written contracts and oral agreements, and the influence activities they undertake. Those that fail to register or omit information face both civil and criminal penalties.

    According to recent reports, all content they disseminate must also bear a foreign-agent label: “a conspicuous statement,” in the statute’s words. The Justice Department sets the rules for what that looks like, and it has not updated them since 2003. In January 2025, the Justice Department proposed amendments to these rules to patch them for the digital age. The proposed amendments would require a label on “each individual post” online, such as on social media platforms, but they do not address AI foreign agents. The final rule should require every message from DeepSeek, Kimi, or Qwen to carry the disclaimer: “This was generated by an agent of the Chinese government and Chinese Communist Party.”.

    Industry observers note that the standard objection is that ordinary citizens do not read disclosures. That may be true of long medical forms or Securities and Exchange Commission filings, but this label would be short. And disclosure works because experts—investors, journalists, researchers—read filings and react. When researchers and lawmakers flagged gaps in China Daily’s FARA filings, the Chinese media tech giant disclosed that it had paid millions of dollars to The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post to publish its propaganda. Payments to the Journal ended that same month. Forcing Chinese AI companies to register under FARA would also shed light on how far Chinese AI is spreading so that Americans can decide, with real data, whether they want further action, such as a ban.

    American companies that use Chinese AI models can also become foreign agents if they fall under a foreign principal’s “direction or control” and engage in activities subject to FARA. This could happen in two ways: the manufacturer serves as a “CCP spokesperson,” or as a “CCP executive.”.

    Industry observers note that in the first, an American tech giant takes an unmodified Chinese AI model and lets Americans discuss political problems with it—say, via a video game character or a customer service chatbot. The model returns its usual propaganda, so the company has effectively hired a CCP spokesperson. Accordingly, it must label its outputs. Both the Justice Department and a federal court have found that rebroadcasting unmodified programming from the Russian state outlet Sputnik turns an American company into a foreign agent. Of course, American companies can avoid FARA obligations if they do not engage in any of the activities listed by the statute, such as discussing politics. A company whose public-facing Chinese AI model discusses only, say, hotel check-in times, not politics, would not be a CCP spokesperson.

    According to recent reports, in the second scenario, an American firm outsources so much of its decision-making to an unmodified Chinese AI model that it has effectively hired a CCP executive. If a company hired a brilliant human strategist who always pushed Beijing’s interests, and the company followed that advice, FARA would apply. The same logic holds if an American company cedes control to the Chinese government by giving Beijing’s models high decision-making authority. Although it may sound fantastical, 64 percent of chief executives surveyed in IBM’s 2026 CEO Study say they already feel comfortable making major strategic decisions based on AI input; overall, CEOs expect AI to make 48 percent of routine operational decisions autonomously by 2030. An American company that wants to avoid becoming a CCP executive must be sure not to fall under the direction or control of such models. The Justice Department should update its 2020 guidance on what constitutes “direction or control,” spelling out how much decision-making a company can outsource to AI before it has effectively hired a “CCP executive.”.

    American companies could attempt to train away the party bias in the Chinese AI models they adopt, but it is unclear whether that is even possible. Perplexity, an American AI organization, trained DeepSeek to stop ignoring questions about the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre and about human rights abuses in Xinjiang, but that does not fix the deeper problem of corrupt chains of thought. As these models get more capable, Chinese AI companies may also find cleverer ways to hide instructions. Or they could just stick them in the contract: some recent DeepSeek licenses prohibit modifying models to generate “inappropriate content” under Chinese law, making propaganda part of the deal. If research reveals that companies can reliably remove the bias, the Justice Department and the Commerce Department should issue standards on how to train away FARA liability.

    Although Pam Bondi, then the U.S. attorney general, limited criminal FARA charges in 2025 to “conduct similar to more traditional espionage by foreign government actors,” Attorney General Todd Blanche’s Justice Department indicates it is considering a fresh rule to “keep pace with technological change.” It should include AI foreign agents.

    Of course, Washington should wield FARA’s expansive authorities with care. Frivolous prosecutions under the statute could stifle democracy. Other countries have used foreign-agent laws to shut down civil society. Since 2022, Russia has barred anyone it deems a foreign agent from holding office and organizing public events. Still, FARA is a far narrower statute, and it should stay that way. It reaches only those acting under the direction or control of a foreign principal, and it simply requires registration and labeling, leaving the speaker free to keep speaking. Chinese AI companies that are required by law to promote the CCP’s interests fit squarely within what Congress had in mind when it approved FARA in 1938.

    Recent findings suggest that FARA can help in the United States, but the problem is global. Chinese AI is spreading rapidly in Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East. That is no accident. In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping unveiled the World AI Cooperation Organization, a Shanghai-based group of 29 countries meant to make AI “beneficial, safe, and fair,” along with a development initiative to export Chinese AI worldwide. The United States and its allies cannot allow CCP executives and spokespeople to run the world’s companies and governments.

    It has been revealed that unfortunately, the American alternatives are not particularly attractive. The most capable U.S. models are far more expensive, are largely unmodifiable, and may contain their own biases. That is why the United States and its allies should create an AI compact rooted in transparency, with standards that make countries comfortable adopting allied models as their own. These should include freedom from state ideological mandates, disclosure of how the models were trained to be helpful and safe, and independent auditing.

    Every member of such a compact should also adopt FARA’s wisdom by mandating labels on government-directed AI, and the United States should hold American AI companies to those transparency standards. The bloc should then release models that match China’s in price and quality (that is, around seven months behind the American frontier). Allied governments can help pay for computing power and electricity, assist in clearing regulatory hurdles, and make bulk purchase commitments to bring prices down. American companies may cut prices on their older models on their own to compete with Chinese models. If they do not, lower prices for those worse models should be the condition for the public support they receive, such as federal contracts and permission to lease federal land for data centers, just as a pharmaceutical company can charge high prices for only a set period before generic drugs arrive. The compact’s members should also use export loans and guarantees to steer developing countries toward allied AI.

    Recent findings suggest that by welcoming supposedly free technology from China, the United States and its allies have unwittingly invited countless foreign agents to their shores. The Foreign Agents Registration Act can strip away the disguise, and an allied AI compact can give the world a better offer.

    Trump, while wielding veto threat, sees possible deals with incoming Dem majority

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • President Donald Trump stated Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.
    • After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    President Donald Trump, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, gestures during a news conference in the White House briefing room on Friday (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    President Donald Trump stated Friday he might get more accomplished with Democrats running the House and Senate than he did in a Republican-led Congress, but his legislative to-do list differs significantly from the incoming majority party.

    After previously suggesting he could strike a bipartisan immigration deal with Democrats, Trump on Friday added several items to his wish list after returning Thursday night from a swing across Asia, including several that have support with Democrats with whom he’s bitterly clashed before.

    Sources indicate that speaking in a stuffy James A. Brady Briefing Room for just shy of 90 minutes, the GOP president contended, without naming a single Democratic leader or lawmaker, that members of the opposition party have called him “about two things in particular,” pointing to health care and immigration.

    “What's happened is I've been called by a lot of Democrats,” he remarked of the 17 days since Democrats gained dozens of seats across the two chambers. “But people that matter, people that have a lot to do, and they want to talk to me.”.

    But Trump also reminded Democrats that he is more than willing to veto legislation he doesn’t agree with, calling it one of the “extreme powers” of his office and one he might use to bring them to the bargaining table.

    “So they’re going to send things my way, and I’m going to veto them. And then they’re going to send more things, and I’m going to veto them,” he noted. “I think, after a month or so, they’re going to send things, and I’m going to say, ’I’m going to veto, unless you want to do this and this and this.”.

    According to recent reports, he predicted House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely upcoming speaker of the House, and Sen. Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., expected to become majority leader, would seek deals because both are “smart.” He would not say if he’d spoken to either leader, but called Jeffries “streetwise,” while noting he had once made a donation to Schumer earlier in their careers.

    Trump went as far as to suggest working across the aisle on health care “may be easier than the Republicans trying to ram it through in reconciliation,” a reference to a fast-track process that allows sprawling bills to pass each chamber with a simple majority — legislation typically needs 60 votes to advance in the Senate.

    The sports-loving president added the Senate-approved “Protect College Sports Act” to his list, and repeated his support for legislation to make Hollywood production companies more competitive. The House moved closer Friday to acting on an amended “Protect” bill when the Rules Committee posted a notice calling for any desired floor amendments by noon on Wednesday.

    “We have to pass that bill,” Trump noted. “Every college is going to go bankrupt if we don't get a bill because they're going crazy.”.

    The Senate’s “Protect” bill would establish the first federal regulatory framework for college athletics, setting national rules for name, image and likeness deals and compensation, as well as installing limitations on agents. It would put in place standards for NIL agreements, create guidelines for schools making direct payments to athletes and provide targeted antitrust protections to certain governing organizations.

    According to recent reports, he said the Senate bill has “tremendous bipartisan support,” but its path in the House remains unclear, according to lobbyists who have worked on the issue. That’s because some House conservatives oppose it and the Congressional Black Caucus has said its members would vote “no.”.

    The CBC has linked it to GOP efforts to redistrict majority minority districts in states the group, with its nearly 60 House members, contends would benefit most from the bill. The CBC is expected to be even larger in the next Congress, further complicating the “Protect” bill’s path to Trump’s desk.

    Recent findings suggest that trump also pointed to the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act as another possible bipartisan bill. The legislation would establish a federal tax credit to encourage film and television productions to shoot in the United States rather than overseas. Some countries offer American film companies lucrative production incentives to shoot on their soil.

    In a twist, Trump noted Sen. Adam B. Schiff — a longtime foe from the California Democrat’s days probing the president’s alleged ties to Russia as House Intelligence Committee chair during Trump 1.0 — supports that measure.

    “It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support. I tell you what, Adam Schiff mentioned, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’”.

    But the president’s vision of a 120th Congress bipartisan agenda differs from what Democrats have promised.

    Many Democratic incumbents and candidates promised voters they would pursue legislation to lower consumer prices, pare health care costs and end Trump’s Iran conflict, which the president again on Friday acknowledged hurt his party by increasing prices.

    Jeffries, during a press conference in Washington on Nov. 4, pointed to reversing the administration’s Medicaid cuts, reviving the Affordable Care Act credits, ending the war and lowering costs as his conference’s “North Star” priorities. This week he also said he would seek to move an immigration-related bill “immediately,” and that the House would “hold the crooks accountable,” a nod to aggressive oversight both chambers are likely to engage in.

    Recent findings suggest that on Iran, reporters pressed Vice President JD Vance over his post-midterms X post blaming the war for the GOP wipeout. One reporter pressed Vance, a potential 2028 Republican presidential hopeful, whether he — like Trump — would start the conflict again. Vance sidestepped as he approached the lectern from behind Trump’s right shoulder, but did not give a full-throated endorsement to go to war again.

    It has been revealed that “The president has said he would do it again,” Vance replied. “And my view is that my goal is, and my job is to support the president of the United States.”.

    In a potential 2028 GOP primary preview, Secretary of State Marco Rubio — who has gained ground in some polls since the midterms — was expressionless as he stood a few feet away, positioned behind Trump’s left shoulder.

    Industry observers note that trump’s midday press conference marked his first since voters handed Democrats at least 258 House seats and 56 in the Senate come Jan. 3. He again contended the outcome would have been different “if I were on the ballot,” and floated vague conspiracy theories about some falling prices since Democratic candidates bulldozed across the country.

    It has been revealed that at one point, he decided to make an announcement that he claimed he had not warned his staff about by floating a threat to U.S. companies that want to build data centers overseas.

    ​"We're going to put a tremendous tax on them, if they do it," he noted, continuing his advocacy of erecting the unpopular facilities across the United States and willingness to use executive powers.

    Industry observers note that as he returned to Washington Thursday night, the White House touted on social media what it called $17 billion in new deals secured with Asian countries this week. Trump on Friday claimed he told Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. his country would begin buying “100 percent” of its oil from the United States — and Marcos had said, “Yes, sir.”.

    White House aides handed out a one-page “declaration toward peace” before Trump arrived that he later said he had reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

    The three leaders agreed to ramp up production of petroleum products, pursue unspecified changes to the United Nations and a statement that a “nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought,” according to the White House’s description of the declaration.

    It also included a line about agreement on the “principle of state consent and respect for immunities of state officials,” an apparent show of support to Putin being targeted by international criminal entities over his conduct of his war with Ukraine. The U.S. president on Friday said such entities have “fake power.”.

    Industry observers note that trump called the declaration “formal,” as he lauded Chinese cities he was driven through this week as extremely “clean.” He compared them to some Democratic-run U.S. cities and states he described as “so embarrassing” and “dirty.” He dubbed Xi, considered by many Republican and Democratic lawmakers to be a dictator, a “great man.”.

    Some Republican lawmakers who will return for the 120th Congress said they have some reservations about Trump meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts, doubting Putin’s and Xi’s sincerity about changing course on a number of challenges.

    Retiring Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., went further Thursday.

    “Traditionally, Republicans stood up to Russia and to China. And we stood up for freedom, and we stood up for countries that shared our values,” Bacon, who has floated a potential 2028 presidential bid, said during a National Press Club event. “President Trump has been terrible on this right here.".

    “He has played footsie with Putin, he’s even blaming Zelenskyy for why the war started,” he added, referring to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. “It infuriates me. And Ronald Reagan is rolling in his grave. … And now the Democrats are talking about the bad Russians and the bad Chinese, and we got to be tougher — it’s another role reversal, here.”.
