    • The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.
    • The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

    The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

    Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

    The highlights this week: The presidents of China, Russia, and the United States hold a historic trilateral summit in Shenzhen, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi receives a cold welcome in China, and fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s scandal continues.

    The first-ever trilateral meeting among the leaders of China, Russia, and the United States—held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering this week in Shenzhen, China—was, as expected, little more than a photo opportunity.

    According to recent reports, still, all three will be pleased with the pictures. U.S. President Donald Trump, smarting from his party’s overwhelming defeat in the midterm elections, gets to play statesman. Russian President Vladimir Putin gets to play peacemaker. And Chinese President Xi Jinping gets to play the man in charge—though nowadays that may be more accurate than not.

    The official joint statement from the summit, issued by Chinese state news agency Xinhua, echoed themes that Xi has promoted throughout Trump’s second term: strategic stability, opposition to Cold War thinking and economic decoupling, and respect for the outcomes of World War II.

    Recent findings suggest that china and Russia routinely trot out that final point to justify their territorial claims today. The irony is rich for China, which was represented during the war by leaders of the Republic of China government, who later fled to Taiwan. (In Eastern Europe, meanwhile, the victorious power was the Soviet Union, not Russia.).

    Before the meeting, there was talk that the Shenzhen trilateral might amount to a new Yalta Conference—the 1945 summit at which the three main victors of World War II divided up Europe.

    In a recent development, this speculation drew on the long-simmering idea that the world might once again be carved into spheres of influence. But the idea that a fresh Yalta is possible at all is fundamentally misguided. Two of the three great powers today are bogged down in economically devastating wars of choice against smaller countries.

    Crucially, it is clear that the world is not theirs to divide. Trump cannot force Ukraine to surrender or hand Taiwan to Beijing. Putin cannot restore Soviet grandeur by force. And China, for all its bluster, has yet to bring Taiwan to heel.

    The Yalta fantasy also ignores how much weaker today’s great powers are than their 1945 counterparts. At the time, the Soviet military was the largest in the world, the U.S. economy was bigger than those of the rest of the developed world combined, and the diminished United Kingdom still ruled an empire that encompassed one-quarter of the global population.

    Nor did the Yalta bargain of a world divided among superpowers hold. Rather than securing a lasting peace, it laid the groundwork for the Cold War and spawned bloodshed from Korea to Hungary within a few years. A grand bargain among China, Russia, and the United States today is even less likely to work.

    For all the talk of a new world order, the summit produced little of substance. The three powers nominally agreed to engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks, but with no advance diplomatic work and significant differences among their arsenals, not much will come of it.

    Sources indicate that the joint statement did have one effect, though. The leaders’ condemnation of the International Criminal Court handed China and Russia ideological ammunition, reinforcing the autocratic disdain for international institutions and human rights that all countries are meant to uphold.

    According to recent reports, but Beijing should not mistake the summit for a license to keep the terms of U.S.-China talks strictly about power. With Democrats set to take control of key China-related committees in the U.S. Congress in January, issues involving democracy and political dissidents will take on renewed importance, no matter what Trump or Xi would prefer.

    Sources indicate that takaichi receives cold welcome. Hosting the APEC gathering gave China another opportunity to signal its displeasure with Japan. The bilateral relationship is still at a nadir, more than a year after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi noted a Chinese invasion of Taiwan could justify Japanese intervention.

    Recent findings suggest that as other leaders were greeted with fanfare, Takaichi was received at Shenzhen’s airport by a relatively low-ranking diplomat. I suspect there was also implicit misogyny at play: Chinese state media has denigrated Takaichi in sexist terms, as it did with former Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen.

    Though Takaichi was largely sidelined at the APEC meeting, she did what she could to meet bilaterally with other leaders instead.

    According to recent reports, A magisterial China resource. Last month, scholar Endymion Wilkinson published the eighth edition of Chinese History: A New Manual, one of the most crucial books in the field of China studies. First published in 1973 as a relatively slim research guide of around 70,000 words, it now approaches 2 million and covers everything from Chinese cuisine to politics.

    Recent findings suggest that wilkinson is now 85, but each latest edition still contains substantial revisions and additions. The latest includes personal recollections from his stints in China: first as an English teacher at Peking University on the eve of the Cultural Revolution and later as the European Union’s ambassador from 1994 to 2001.

    A remarkable work of erudition and dedication, the book remains a starting point for virtually any research into China.

    Nvidia scandal updates. The fallout from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s marital infidelities continues to widen, with the organization facing legal scrutiny and a wider crackdown on U.S. chip exports. Huang had an affair with alleged Chinese asset Alice Huang; he resigned from his role last week and is set to testify before the U.S. Congress early next month.

    According to recent reports, reporting suggests that Nvidia’s involvement in networks designed to evade U.S. export controls lies somewhere between active complicity and willful blindness. Alice Huang’s husband, who reportedly knew about the affair, also played a major part in building state-backed data centers designed to give China access to more computing power.

    Alice Huang is now back in Beijing, beyond the reach of potential criminal charges in Singapore.

    U.S. cybersecurity risks? As many tech services seemed to break in the last week, many people asked whether the outages were an ordinary screwup or a cyberattack. The consensus so far is that the problems were unrelated, caused by companies rushing to upgrade systems before the holidays.

    But it’s worth remembering that China achieved deep penetration of U.S. infrastructure with Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored hacking group, which was publicly exposed in 2024. The Trump administration dismantled the expert groups investigating Volt Typhoon early last year, and China could likely still shut down large parts of U.S. life if it chose to do so.

    James Palmer is a deputy editor at Foreign Policy. Bluesky: @beijingpalmer.bsky.social.

    House Democrats unveiled a 2027 legislative calendar Friday that includes 33 voting weeks, as the incoming majority party looks to pass an ambitious agenda following massive midterm election wins.

    According to the calendar released by soon-to-be House Majority Leader Katherine M. Clark, the chamber would convene for the first session of the 120th Congress with a rare Sunday gathering on Jan. 3. The first votes of the year would take place that week.

    “House Democrats are hitting the ground running on January 3,” the Massachusetts Democrat stated in a statement. “This calendar reflects the scale and urgency of our work ahead. Americans voted for a Majority that will move decisively to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable. Whether we’re working in DC or in our districts, that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”.

    In a recent development, in most months, the House will be in session for three weeks, with the exception of the annual August recess. That will be followed by four consecutive weeks of voting in September.

    The calendar also includes a two-week break for Easter in March, while the Fourth of July falls on a Sunday.

    The 33-week schedule suggests a jam-packed year for the House, following a year in which the chamber saw dozens of canceled session days because of floor impasses and a record-long partial government shutdown. The struggles of the outgoing Republican majority has even bled into the lame-duck session, with absences by dozens of lawmakers forcing outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., to send a letter to members Friday urging them to “remain fully engaged” in the closing weeks of the 119th Congress.

    With the calendar released, House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of Upcoming York has already outlined some of his top priorities for his presumptive speakership, including an ambitious health care agenda, immigration legislation and aggressive oversight of the Trump administration.

    But even after flipping both chambers of Congress, Democrats face the uphill battle of working with President Donald Trump if they want their agenda signed into law.

    Trump emphasized his “extreme” veto power during a news conference Friday, but he also mentioned he thinks Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., are “smart.”.

    In a recent development, “They're going to send things my way, and I'm going to veto them, and then they're going to send more things, and I'm going to veto them,” he remarked. “I think after a month or so, they're going to send things, and I'm going to say, ‘I'm going to veto unless you want to do this and this and this.’".

    The Senate calendar for next year has not yet been released.

    According to recent reports, these worries are entirely justified; Trump has a track record of cozying up to autocrats and turning his back on democratic allies. Should he sit down with Xi and Putin, he must avoid selling out European and Asian partners who will not be at the table. And given the three leaders’ headstrong personalities and competing national interests that pit the United States against what Xi calls a “no limits” partnership between China and Russia, the meeting might ultimately yield little progress on major issues.

    Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, Trump would be right to join a summit with Xi and Putin. No U.S. president has ever held a trilateral meeting with the leaders of China and Russia, and the proposed talks would break the ice and begin to normalize much-needed dialogue. Authoritarianism is not going away, so autocracies and democracies must learn not only to live comfortably alongside one another but also to work together to tame geopolitical rivalry and tackle global challenges in an interdependent world. Americans will not find it easy to get along with the likes of Russia and China, whose political systems threaten the U.S. commitment to spreading democracy. But Trump is taking a bold step in the right direction by engaging with the heads of the world’s leading autocracies.

    Sources indicate that if he meets with Xi and Putin, Trump should aim low and focus on making meaningful, if limited, progress on a small number of core problems that could benefit from a three-way conversation: the flash points of the Korean Peninsula, Ukraine, and Iran, as well as arms control and strategic stability. But even if the summit yields no concrete results, it will nonetheless have been worthwhile. Trump, Xi, and Putin are paving the way for their successors to advance great-power cooperation across ideological lines and stabilize a fragmented world.

    According to recent reports, I have argued previously, including in a 2021 Foreign Affairs essay with Richard Haass, that a global concert—an informal steering group of great powers modeled on the nineteenth-century Concert of Europe—offers the best hope of curbing geopolitical competition and enabling collective action in a multipolar world. In addition to the United States, China, and Russia, a latest concert would include India, Japan, the European Union, and representatives from Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Concerts sacrifice representation for efficacy and give only the geopolitically influential states that must be there a seat at the table. They set aside ideological differences and bring democracies and autocracies together to focus on international cooperation. Because concerts eschew binding, enforceable procedures in favor of informal consensus building, they can succeed when formal institutions such as the UN Security Council are paralyzed and when the United States wavers in its commitment to rules-based multilateralism.

    But the time has not come for a global concert. Concerts function effectively only when their members are committed to the territorial status quo, are willing to exercise strategic restraint and pursue mutual benefits, and are ready to settle disputes diplomatically. Putin’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and Xi’s decision to back Russia have, for now, scuttled hopes that the great powers will normalize restraint and the peaceful settlement of disputes. Meanwhile, Trump’s “America first” statecraft shuns joint action and mutual gain in favor of unilateralism.

    In a recent development, yet even though Trump, Xi, and Putin are the wrong leaders at the wrong time to establish a great-power steering group that other major players would eventually join, Trump’s iconoclastic diplomacy sets a useful precedent. His Alaska summit with Putin last year and two summits with Xi this year were admittedly long on pageantry and short on substance. But by taking the controversial step of pursuing joint talks with the two leaders, Trump is widening the diplomatic Overton window and expanding what is politically possible for future U.S. presidents. Avoiding great-power conflict and taming a world in increasing disarray requires the United States to build constructive relations with both China and Russia. Trump deserves credit for starting a trialogue that his successors can carry forward.

    In a recent development, if they meet in Shenzhen, Trump, Xi, and Putin should focus on easing tensions at key geopolitical flash points. The Korean Peninsula presents the best opportunity for the three leaders to collaborate. At the UN General Assembly in September, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung laid out an ambitious plan for normalizing relations with Pyongyang, including a proposal to replace the peninsula’s 1953 armistice with a “peace regime” that promotes “respect for each other’s systems and acknowledgement of our differences.” As part of that plan, Lee has advocated a phased approach to North Korean denuclearization, with an initial freeze on weapons development followed by gradual reductions in Pyongyang’s arsenal of nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles until the peninsula is denuclearized.

    Lee’s bold proposal could bring U.S., Chinese, and Russian interests into alignment. Trump has made it clear that he wants to de-escalate tensions on the Korean Peninsula and is already seeking a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Beijing and Moscow are competing for influence over Kim, but both want a stable relationship between North and South Korea, so they might be willing to cooperate on proposals to halt nuclear weapons production and encourage talks between Pyongyang and Seoul. Trump, Xi, and Putin should aim to emerge from their meeting with a initiative for advancing Lee’s peace agenda; jointly supporting a freeze on North Korean nuclear weapons development is a good place to start.

    The prospects for progress toward ending the war in Ukraine are much dimmer but not nonexistent. Trump should be striving to weaken Russia’s ability to sustain the war, but he has long resisted tightening sanctions on Moscow. He talks up potential business ventures with Russia and, in recent weeks, even struck a deal with Putin to get more Russian diesel into global markets and waived a latest round of congressional sanctions against Moscow. Trump evidently cares more about trying to bring down fuel prices than about curbing Russia’s ability to fund its war against Ukraine.

    A summit offers Trump the opportunity to change course and try to convince Xi to restrain Putin. Trump has vowed to bring the war in Ukraine to an end, and the Chinese leader can help him achieve that goal. Xi has enormous leverage over Putin: China backs the Kremlin diplomatically, is the largest buyer of Russian oil and gas, and is the main supplier of dual-use items such as semiconductors and machine tools that are critical to Russian weapons manufacturing.

    Xi has played along with Putin’s war against Ukraine so far, presumably because the conflict diverts U.S. attention and resources away from Asia, divides NATO, and allows Xi and Putin to cast themselves as leading a global resistance to Western hegemony. But when Xi and Trump met this May, the leaders agreed to pursue “a constructive relationship of strategic stability” between China and the United States, which Xi could advance by pressing Putin to de-escalate. As more Russians feel the effects of the war, the Kremlin may be newly receptive to such pressure. Ukrainian drone strikes are taking a significant toll on Russia’s oil sector and logistics networks, which means Russian citizens face mounting gas and commodities shortages. Meanwhile, some 35,000 Russian soldiers per month are losing their lives or sustaining severe injuries in eastern Ukraine, forcing Putin to consider the unpopular move of ramping up military mobilization. With no battlefield victory in sight, Putin has reasons to entertain a diplomatic off-ramp.

    Trump and Xi could press Putin to accept a set of limited but consequential steps to de-escalate the conflict. These could include an agreement between Russia and Ukraine—brokered and monitored by Washington and Beijing—to end attacks on energy installations and infrastructure, civilian targets, and commercial shipping. Trump and Xi could also jointly press Putin to refrain from actions that could broaden the war, such as penetrating NATO airspace with Russian drones, sabotaging European infrastructure, and threatening to use nuclear weapons. This pressure, combined with the allure of improving diplomatic and commercial ties to the United States, might convince Putin to relent on at least some of these concerns.

    Sources indicate that trump could also use a trilateral summit to seek help extricating the United States from its war in Iran—a quagmire that has produced regional mayhem and soaring oil prices. As Tehran continues to issue maximalist demands and the war disrupts shipping through the straits of Hormuz and Bab el Mandeb, Trump needs an out.

    Neither Xi nor Putin has yet been inclined to lend a hand. China is still buying Iranian oil and providing Tehran with military intelligence and dual-use items that end up in Iranian drones and missiles, and Russia is providing satellite targeting data, munitions, advanced drone technology, and logistical support. Both Beijing and Moscow are happy to see the United States mired in a conflict that is exacerbating divisions within the American electorate and fracturing NATO.

    Recent findings suggest that as a major energy exporter, Russia benefits from the spike in oil prices that the conflict has triggered, so pressing Putin to cease supporting Iran is likely a lost cause. But China is the world’s largest oil importer, and Beijing has a vested interest in lowering energy prices by stabilizing exports from the Middle East. Although China’s large oil reserves have buffered its economy from rising oil prices so far, those reserves have been significantly depleted. China’s crude oil imports have begun to climb again, leaving its economy exposed to high energy prices if the conflict drags on. And as the world’s largest exporter of goods, China suffers from the dampening effect high energy prices have on global growth.

    It has been revealed that xi might therefore be amenable to helping Trump end the war. Trump should ask Xi to stop or at least slow the flow of Chinese dual-use items to Iran. Washington’s naval blockade and financial and commercial sanctions on Tehran have already taken a toll on Iran’s economy and military supply chains. By cutting off Chinese technology shipments to Iran, Beijing could deepen this economic isolation and help convince Tehran to negotiate an end to the conflict.

    Industry observers note that xi could also press Iran to drop its unrealistic demands for ending the war, including that the United States withdraw its forces from the Gulf, release frozen Iranian assets, and remove economic sanctions. Washington might well be willing to offer economic relief, but only as part of postwar negotiations toward a deal that reins in Iran’s nuclear ambitions. Xi could help clear the way for those talks by urging Iran to accept credible terms for ending the immediate conflict.

    Beyond working to resolve current conflicts, Trump should promote future strategic stability by pursuing arms control negotiations with Xi and Putin. Every arms control agreement negotiated between Washington and Moscow has expired; their final nuclear pact, New START, ended in February. There are at the moment no caps on the American and Russian strategic arsenals and no regular inspections, data exchanges, or notifications of nuclear exercises. This nuclear free-for-all is particularly dangerous given Russia’s nuclear saber rattling amid the war in Ukraine and the Kremlin’s fondness for provocations such as sending explosive-laden drones into NATO airspace.

    In October, Trump appropriately proposed that a trilateral summit include a discussion of nuclear arms control. China has long resisted engaging in arms control talks, arguing that it should not have to limit its nuclear program when its arsenal is much smaller than that of the United States and Russia. But Beijing is rapidly expanding and modernizing its nuclear arsenal. The Pentagon has projected that China will possess more than 1,000 operational warheads by 2030, putting it in nearly the same league as the United States and Russia, which have stockpiles of roughly 1,800 operational warheads each. With the uncertain trajectory of U.S.-Chinese relations, instability on the Korean Peninsula, and China’s tense relationship with Taiwan heightening the risk of conflict in East Asia, Beijing must be part of high-level nuclear arms control discussions.

    Sources indicate that realistically, Trump can do little more than start this conversation and invite Xi and Putin to continue it in future trilateral negotiations led by teams of diplomats and arms control experts. In future talks, the three countries should discuss not only caps on nuclear weapons stockpiles but also military-to-military contacts, crisis management protocols, notifications of military exercises, counterproliferation, and other measures that can contribute to strategic stability.

    In a recent development, trump could add a host of other topics to the summit’s agenda, including trade, energy security, and AI regulation, but he should avoid a wide-ranging conversation that goes nowhere. He might, however, notch an easy win by proposing a three-way initiative in an area in which cooperation is relatively straightforward—for example, a joint medical mission to the Democratic Republic of the Congo to help fight Ebola or a joint aid operation to deliver humanitarian relief to Gaza or Yemen. A concrete, public effort along these lines would show that trilateral dialogue can yield viable cooperation.

    Recent findings suggest that yet Trump should guard against being so eager for a win that he lets Xi and Putin take advantage of him. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit takes place only two weeks after American voters dealt Trump and his party a historic rebuke in the U.S. midterm elections. The notoriously thin-skinned president could be tempted to make concessions to Beijing and Moscow to score a foreign policy breakthrough. He must avoid making a behind-closed-doors compromise on Ukraine that he then tries to force on Kyiv and its European supporters. Similarly, he must hold the line on Taiwan even as he seeks Xi’s help on North Korea, Ukraine, and Iran. Otherwise, Trump will leave the trilateral meeting confirming the worst fears of those who foresaw a latest Yalta in the making. Capitulating to Xi and Putin would alienate Washington’s allies, project American weakness, and erode global deterrence.

    According to recent reports, trump must also carefully manage the optics of a trilateral summit. Putin is an indicted war criminal who continues to prosecute a ruthless war of aggression against Ukraine. It is far too soon to let him out of the penalty box. And although Washington is right to seek a good working relationship with Beijing, it is time for Trump’s “truly great friendship” with Xi to bear fruit. Trump must approach talks with sobriety and pragmatism, seeking to demonstrate that Washington, Beijing, and Moscow can work together to help promote global peace and stability.

    A summit next week will not usher in a new era of great-power collaboration anytime soon. It might not even yield concrete deliverables. Still, the meeting would set a valuable precedent. Simply by sitting down with Xi and Putin, Trump would begin a much-needed trilateral conversation.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As solar and energy storage portfolios grow in both size and complexity, managing performance is just one part of the equation. Owners and operators must also keep track of power purchase agreements (PPAs), warranties, service contracts, billing, compliance requirements and project-level profitability.

    Recent findings suggest that enSights is looking to bring those responsibilities together with the launch of its AI Studio, a new addition to its Energy Business Management (EBM) platform. The manufacturer unveiled the launch Nov. 10.

    The AI Studio is designed to give solar and storage owners, operators, and asset managers access to a customizable team of AI specialists that can support business and operational workflows. Through no-code tools, customers can create AI dashboards and reports using natural-language instructions, while still establishing their own workflows, routines, data-access permissions and approval requirements.

    The approach here reflects a broader shift toward renewable energy software, it’s moving beyond monitoring individual assets toward managing the financial and operational performance of entire portfolios.

    According to enSights, its EBM platform brings together energy management systems (EMS), production data, billing, PPA information, operations and maintenance, contractual obligations and compliance on a unified data foundation. That integration is central to the company’s AI strategy.

    Rather than limiting AI applications to identifying equipment concerns or answering generation-related questions, the platform is designed to connect energy production with the contracts and financial obligations associated with each project.

    According to recent reports, the AI Studio includes an orchestrator that coordinates specialized AI agents focused on areas like monitoring, operations, revenue, warranties, permits, lenders, insurers, and asset management. For portfolio managers, those capabilities could help reduce the time spent reviewing disconnected systems and manually reconciling information across departments. Automated reviews of contractual obligations, revenue performance and operational alerts could also help teams identify issues earlier and direct attention to matters that still require human intervention.

    The enSights AI Studio dashboard provides solar and energy storage operators with AI-powered tools for asset management, operational workflows, and financial oversight. Credit: enSights.

    It has been revealed that enSights emphasized that people remain in control of the AI Team. Users determine which workflows the agents handle and where approvals are required. Physical asset controls remain governed by established EMS and site-level systems.

    The AI Studio also builds on an expanded financial management offering within the EBM platform. Its Financial Asset Management Module includes revenue assurance, contract, and obligation management, and profit-and-loss reporting.

    The module is intended to provide project-level financial visibility, helping companies identify and prevent revenue losses while generating reports for investors.

    The platform also includes real-time EMS, weather and tariff forecasting, along with dispatch planning intended to optimize revenue while maintaining grid safety and local compliance.

    enSights says its platform is deployed globally across more than 100,000 sites, representing over 5 GW of assets. The manufacturer plans to demonstrate the AI Studio and its broader EBM platform at RE+ 2026.

    As AI gains traction across the clean energy industry, the next competitive advantage could come from connecting operational intelligence with the financial and contractual decisions that determine how successfully renewable energy portfolios perform.

    Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at the headliners of this year’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, a ruling of state-sponsored genocide in Myanmar, and Anthropic’s record-setting public debut.

    In a recent development, A week of high-level diplomacy capped off on Thursday with a trilateral summit featuring U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin. But although the meeting, which took place at a sprawling lakeside villa in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, was initially framed as an opportunity to pursue global peacemaking, analysts remarked it proved to be little more than a photo op.

    Heading into the dialogue, Trump was clear about what he hoped to accomplish. “The United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth and also to lessen the risk of those weapons being used,” the U.S. president mentioned at the start of the summit. The three countries hold more than 90 percent of the world’s total nuclear weapons.

    Yet the roughly 70-minute meeting concluded with no mention of future nuclear negotiations or a potential arms reduction treaty. Instead, the three leaders released a peace declaration that “reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.” It was one of just four items listed in the joint statement—and the last one mentioned.

    No. 1 on the list was a commitment to reform the United Nations. The United States, China, and Russia are three of the five permanent members on the U.N. Security Council, granting them significant sway over the international body’s actions. Yet all three nations have repeatedly accused the U.N. of bias.

    The second item remarked the three leaders “initiative to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations” and “reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows.” It did not specify how much additional crude would be provided to help stabilize the market, though the United States has already made efforts to suspend sanctions on Russian oil—to the condemnation of Washington’s Western allies—to ease economic pressures.

    Item three concerned the International Criminal Court (ICC) and similar bodies, with the three leaders arguing that these courts “must not abuse their jurisdiction,” particularly against state officials who they claim have immunity.

    The Trump administration has sought to dismantle the ICC by questioning its status and imposing sanctions on its members; the court is a “rogue globalist organization,” Trump said on Thursday. Putin has similarly denounced the ICC’s authority, particularly after it issued an arrest warrant for him in 2023 citing alleged war crimes. Moscow denies the accusations.

    The trio walked away from Thursday’s meeting with optimistic outlooks. Trump characterized the summit as a “Great and Highly Consequential Trip”; Xi described the talks as “positive, constructive, and fruitful”; and Putin said they were “open and candid.”.

    However, not everyone shared those sentiments. “It’s a historic embarrassment that people will remember long into the future,” U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on Thursday. “It’s a betrayal of the United States by a president who loves nothing more than to bow down to our adversaries for a photo op.”.

    Guilty of genocide. The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday that Myanmar had committed genocide against the country’s minority Rohingya Muslim community beginning in August 2017. This is the first time that the highest U.N. court has found a nation directly responsible for genocide.

    Recent findings suggest that “The court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers,” ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said in the 9-6 ruling. The 15-judge panel, which included 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay, rejected the country’s defense that its so-called “clearance operations” were a legitimate campaign against insurgents.

    Although the ICJ does not have an enforcement mechanism, the landmark decision could help determine future reparations for Rohingya survivors as well as prevent the current junta-led state from casting off its diplomatic pariah status; Myanmar’s military regime has recently tried to rebrand itself as a nominally civilian government.

    Industry observers note that the case, filed by Gambia in 2019, could also impact how the world’s top court handles similar genocide allegations linked to the wars in Gaza and Ukraine. Thursday’s judgment is “a demonstration of international justice & a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand,” U.N. chief António Guterres wrote on X.

    Record IPO. Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday, and already, interest has exceeded expectations. In its initial public offering on Wednesday, the U.S.-based manufacturer behind the artificial intelligence chatbot Claude sold 980 million shares for $83 a pop, raising $83.1 billion. Such a blockbuster showing put Anthropic above SpaceX, the previous debut record-holder, to become the largest stock market opener in history.

    On Thursday, the AI company began trading shares for the first time. It opened at $111.50 per share, pushing Anthropic’s market value to roughly $2 trillion.

    Since Anthropic was founded in 2021, global interest in AI has skyrocketed, with the United States and China leading the charge. Trump has characterized its advancement as akin to the Industrial Revolution, and Xi has similarly invested tens of billions of dollars in its development. AI has become a growing component of modern warfare, driven global markets, and raised security and environmental concerns.

    Recent findings suggest that but as AI has become more powerful, some have begun to warn that the world should pull back. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei led calls in September to place guardrails on the tech’s advancement after former Anthropic employees warned of security risks. “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models,” Amodei wrote at the time. “Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems.”.

    According to recent reports, trump’s Greenland win. Danish lawmakers unanimously approved a security deal on Thursday that will allow the United States to strengthen its presence in Greenland and the wider Arctic region. The deal, which expands on a 1951 defense agreement between the United States and Denmark, aims to defuse months of tensions over the Trump administration’s repeated threats to seize the semiautonomous, mineral-rich territory of Greenland.

    Recent findings suggest that “We have been through a difficult time, during which many people here at home have been concerned about our country and our future,” Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen wrote on Facebook on Thursday. “I hope that today’s decision will help bring greater calm and a sense of security.”.

    Recent findings suggest that first announced in September, the new deal will allow the U.S. military to construct more bases on Greenland, “modernize and expand” its activities at Pituffik Space Base, and set up “defense areas” to bolster its Golden Dome ambitions. In exchange, the territory will remain under Danish control, and Greenland will respect its commitments to the United States if it chooses to seek independence.

    One of the most anticipated video game releases is finally here. Grand Theft Auto VI rolled out at midnight on Thursday, starting in Upcoming Zealand and moving across time zones from Tokyo to London before finally reaching Miami—the inspiration for the game’s Vice City. More than 19 million copies of the open-world action-adventure game have already been sold, amounting to roughly $1.84 billion. Experts anticipate the game’s nearly 100 missions—in which players inhabit the world of a Bonnie and Clyde-like crime duo—to take around 50 hours to complete, so don’t be concerned if you don’t hear from your gamer friends over the next few days.

    #42367. La última oportunidad para la paz

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4568 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Foreignaffairs ↗ Open Full Page

    La última oportunidad para la paz

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

    ⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.
    • En algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable.
    • According to recent reports, no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

    Cómo evitar otra guerra mundial.

    En algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

    According to recent reports, no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

    Pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

    Sources indicate that en las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

    In a recent development, este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

    Recent findings suggest that el éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

    Los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

    Recent findings suggest that en las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

    According to recent reports, hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

    Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

    According to recent reports, nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

    Aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

    Industry observers note that al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

    La integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

    Recent findings suggest that en conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

    It has been revealed that los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

    Sources indicate that en este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

    Sources indicate that pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

    Las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

    La guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

    It has been revealed that por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

    According to recent reports, el mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

    Pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

    It has been revealed that españa ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

    Desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

    According to recent reports, disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

    Los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

    Industry observers note that invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

    Los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

    In a recent development, reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

    Sources indicate that algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

    Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

    El sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

    Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

    Fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

    La primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

    También hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

    In a recent development, un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

    Otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

    Sources indicate that pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

    It has been revealed that la tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

    Por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

    Industry observers note that la reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

    In a recent development, frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

    Industry observers note that en última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

    In a recent development, las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

    Por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

    Sources indicate that un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

    Sources indicate that the Iran war appears to be heating up (again), as diplomatic talks have hit a wall (again). The United States and Iran resumed strikes over the past week, ending a roughly two-month lull in the conflict.

    The renewed fighting has come as Iran continues to attack shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and amid an ongoing U.S. blockade on Iranian oil exports.

    Tit-for-tat. Over the past six days, Iran introduced a series of strikes on U.S. assets in Bahrain, which hosts the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet, and an air base in Kuwait that hosts U.S. forces.

    Iran targeted a U.S. early warning radar facility in Bahrain on Friday and took aim at a radar system at a helicopter base in the tiny island nation on Sunday. No damage was reported. Tehran remarked the attacks were in retaliation for U.S. strikes on Iranian communications towers as well as ongoing drone surveillance operations.

    Sources indicate that on Tuesday, Iran targeted another radar facility in Bahrain with drones, which were reportedly intercepted; the United States retaliated with a strike on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island. Iran responded on Wednesday with an attack on Ali Al Salem air base in Kuwait. There were no reports of damage. Bahrain also said it intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on Wednesday.

    Recent findings suggest that under pressure. U.S. President Donald Trump has been vague about his plans in the war, and some reports suggest he is mulling over ordering expansive strikes.     Trump’s comments came as Israel is reportedly pressing the White House to escalate with a fresh bombing campaign. Roman Gofman, the director of the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad, visited Washington this week, where he is said to have expressed concerns to U.S. officials over alleged Iranian chemical weapons development.

    The United States also has intelligence that Iran has drawn up plans to potentially use a dirty bomb or chemical weapon in Washington, according to a CNN report. Trump on Tuesday stated the United States was looking into the dirty bomb report and takes it “very seriously.” But he later downplayed the prospect of Iran actually using such a weapon in Washington, and he warned that “if it does happen, we’ll wipe them out.” Trump this week also told Fox News there’s “indication that Iran is looking at gasses, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear.”.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, explains why the group opposed Heidi Overton’s FDA confirmation without commitments from the Trump administration to restore in-person dispensing requirements for abortion drugs and address concerns about the agency’s mifepristone safety study.

    A leading pro-life group mentioned it opposed advancing Heidi Overton's nomination to lead the Food and Drug Administration without commitments from the Trump administration on abortion drug policy. The White House withdrew her nomination this week amid questions about her support in the Senate.

    In an interview with Fox News Digital, Erik Baptist, senior vice president of legal strategy at Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, remarked his group asked the Senate to hold up Overton’s confirmation until it received "firm commitments" from the administration on two fronts regarding abortion drug policy.

    Baptist noted the group wants the next FDA nominee to commit to ending mail-order access to abortion drugs authorized under the Biden administration and changing how the agency studies the safety of those pills.

    "Right now, we’re seeing more abortions in this country than before the Supreme Court’s decision overturning Roe v. Wade," Baptist said. "That’s precisely because of what the Biden FDA did to authorize mail-order abortion drugs. We’re seeing upwards of 15,000 abortion drugs and abortions occurring in pro-life states. Those states can’t meaningfully enforce their laws while this nationwide policy is in place.".

    WHITE HOUSE PULLS TRUMP'S FDA PICK HEIDI OVERTON ON EVE OF SENATE PANEL VOTE.

    According to recent reports, the White House stated Heidi Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination. (Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg via Getty Images).

    "Under the Biden-era policy, anybody can obtain these drugs online and receive them through the mail," he continued. "When I say anybody, we’ve seen news story after news story every week about men and other predators obtaining these drugs to coerce or poison women into taking them against their will. Until that policy changes, no pregnant woman is safe from these drugs. My question to this administration is: How many more women have to be poisoned or coerced with abortion drugs before you take action on this drug?".

    Under the Biden administration, the FDA eliminated the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, allowing it to be prescribed without an in-person visit by certified prescribers and dispensed by certified pharmacies through the mail.

    On the group's second point of concern, Baptist said the FDA needs to conduct a new study to show the safety — or lack thereof — of mifepristone.

    "The problem is that the study is significantly flawed," he stated. "It’s almost designed to fail and not lead to future changes to the drug regimen. We have asked for more robust data because significant information is right now lacking, including transparency into the agency’s methodology and an invitation for outside experts who have studied this drug over the last few decades.".

    "This is something that should be bipartisan. Everybody should support better data, more transparency and outside experts who can inform an agency that has never conducted such a study before," he added.

    Several pro-life groups and Republican lawmakers have urged the Trump administration to complete the FDA’s safety review of mifepristone and consider reinstating safeguards, while some have called for removing the drug from the market.

    The FDA said the review is ongoing, with study results expected in December 2026 and a final report expected by March 2027.

    The White House pulled Overton’s nomination to lead the FDA earlier this week, one day before a Senate committee vote. President Donald Trump picked Overton, a physician and White House advisor, in August to succeed Marty Makary, who resigned from the position in May.

    Kyle Diamantas has led the agency in an acting capacity since Makary’s departure.

    WOMAN WHO SAYS ABORTION PILLS NEARLY KILLED HER URGES RFK JR TO ACT AS GROUP DEMANDS MAIL-ORDER CRACKDOWN.

    Heidi Overton appeared alongside President Donald Trump in the Oval Office as he signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images).

    Overton also previously served as vice chair and chief policy officer at the America First Policy Institute, a conservative think tank, where she criticized expanded access to abortion pills in a 2023 policy brief.

    The White House mentioned Overton lacked the votes on Capitol Hill and pulled her nomination, although Sen. Bill Cassidy, chair of the Senate health committee, contended that he believed she could have been confirmed.

    Recent findings suggest that "The White House abandoned a viable confirmation path for Dr. Overton. The WH remarked that this was because she did not have the votes to pass. This was odd as I was having productive conversations with members," Cassidy, R-La., wrote on X. "I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate.".

    Baptist said he did not know whether the White House was concerned about pro-life votes or other constituencies but thinks Cassidy "was making progress with the administration to secure the commitments we were seeking and asking the Senate to hold the administration accountable for.".

    Cassidy had criticized Overton for supporting Trump’s decision to recommend changes to the childhood vaccine schedule, but the senator said he had been convinced she was right for the job after she committed to "follow the science." She had appeared alongside Trump in the Oval Office as the president signed an executive order calling for changes to childhood vaccine recommendations, including a recommendation to administer measles, mumps and rubella vaccines separately once individual shots become available domestically.

    Cassidy stated at a September hearing that there was no scientific evidence for Trump’s suggestion that the combined shot could be "quite lethal" and warned the remark could discourage vaccination.

    "Yes, senator, the MMR vaccine is safe and effective," Overton told Cassidy.

    Pressed on what she would do if Trump asked her to disregard the FDA’s safety standards, Overton said she would give the president her best advice and follow the legal requirements for reviewing individual products.

    Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., asked Overton directly whether Trump was wrong. Overton reiterated that the vaccine was safe and effective and called it the best tool available during the measles outbreak. Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., questioned why she had not corrected Trump in the Oval Office.

    "Why should we expect you to stand up to the president as FDA commissioner?" Markey asked.

    It has been revealed that senate Health Committee Chairman Sen. Bill Cassidy remarked he believed Heidi Overton could have been confirmed to lead the FDA. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images).

    Baptist stated he wants the next FDA commissioner to be somebody who "understands science" and has experience managing an agency.

    "The FDA is a very large bureaucracy with multiple constituencies, so understanding how science is conducted and how drugs are approved will be essential to any successful candidate or nominee for the position," he noted.

    But, Baptist stated, the administration does not have to wait for an FDA nominee to take the position before it can take the action on abortion pill policy that his group desires.

    According to recent reports, "The good news is that it doesn’t have to be the nominee who makes these commitments. The administration can do it because it has admitted that it can take these actions immediately using its own authority," he argued. "That power is within the administration’s possession. It’s a matter of political will, not legal ability.".

    "With regard to fixing the study, I think they can make those changes now," Baptist continued. "They don’t need to wait for a confirmation, especially when they’re saying they’re going to finish the study in December of this year. We might not have an FDA commissioner at that point, or even a nominee. So they need to fix it immediately and course-correct the study before it’s fatally flawed and completed next year.".

    Fox News' Stepheny Price contributed to this report.
